name: AverageHumidity
represents: Average atmospheric humidity across the planet surface (a continuous scalar field, low = arid, high = humid)
decode_recipe: Build the matplotlib viridis LUT (256 entries × 3 uint8). For each pixel RGB, compute squared Euclidean distance to all 256 LUT entries and take the nearest-index i. Scalar = i / 255, giving a normalized humidity fraction in [0, 1]. Note: the anomalously large olive-khaki cluster (~63,57,9) at 33% of pixels sits around viridis index 60–70; verify by checking that visually bright-yellow coastal/wet zones decode near 1.0 and dark-purple continental interiors decode near 0. The bright-yellow extreme (254,231,36) matches viridis[255] = (253,231,37) to within 1 DN, confirming the ramp. If full LUT inversion gives poor residuals, fall back to luminance proxy L = (0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B) / 255 as a monotonic ordinal for rainfall weighting — precision loss is acceptable for that use.
value_semantics: Dark purple/black (≈viridis index 0) = minimum humidity (dry continental interiors or arid zones). Olive-green (dominant, ~index 60–70) = moderate humidity — the modal land-surface state. Cyan-teal = moderately high. Bright yellow (≈viridis index 255, value 254,231,36) = maximum humidity. No legend or physical unit is visible in the image; range is likely a normalized [0,1] fraction or a relative scale internal to the Gleba generator. No explicit sea/ocean distinction; oceans appear at moderate-to-high humidity values in this map.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1 aspect ratio, confirmed by analyzer)
integration_notes: Load as the optional rainfall map in Project-R's erosion stage. Decode via viridis LUT inversion (or luminance proxy) to produce a [0,1] per-pixel runoff weight. Crop and reproject to the Hammer section the same way the heightmap is treated; resampling is safe since the field is spatially smooth. Wire the scalar directly into the K_precip / discharge accumulation weight so wetter areas concentrate river incision. The map does not need to drive K_sp or uplift. It is also a reasonable biome-selection guidance layer (yellow/cyan zones = lush, worth selecting for river-heavy sections; dark-purple zones = arid, fewer rivers expected).
caveats: 1. Humidity ≠ precipitation directly — coastal upwelling zones and rain-shadow highlands can have similar humidity but very different rainfall; if the export set includes an AverageRainfall or Precipitation map, prefer that as the rainfall driver. 2. The dark-olive cluster (63,57,9) at 33% of all pixels is anomalous for mid-viridis (which should be blue-teal at that index range); the Gleba generator may use a custom or non-standard colormap, so validate the decode on a few known-wet and known-dry pixels before relying on the scalar. 3. 8-bit depth gives at most 256 distinct levels — adequate for a runoff weighting field but introduces visible banding if rendered as a direct display overlay. 4. No ice-age vs. present-day variant distinction is apparent; if the export set contains both, check which climatological epoch this represents before pairing with a glacial erosion pass.

name: AverageRainfall
represents: Average planetary precipitation (rainfall intensity) encoded as a viridis colormap ramp across a 4096x2048 equirectangular projection. Yellow-green = high rainfall (equatorial ITCZ band), dark purple = low/arid zones (subtropical highs and rain shadows).
decode_recipe: 1. Build the matplotlib viridis LUT: `import matplotlib.cm as cm; lut = (cm.get_cmap('viridis', 256)(range(256))[:, :3] * 255).astype(np.uint8)` — this gives a (256,3) uint8 array. 2. For each pixel (r,g,b) in the PNG, find the nearest LUT entry by minimising sum-of-squared RGB distance: `idx = np.argmin(np.sum((lut - pixel)**2, axis=1))`. 3. Scalar value = idx / 255.0, giving a float in [0, 1] where 0 = minimum rainfall and 1 = maximum rainfall. 4. No physical units are labelled (no colorbar present); the scalar is relative only. If absolute mm/yr is needed, cross-reference another export asset that contains the scale. No LUT inversion is required — viridis runs dark-to-bright low-to-high, matching the rainfall direction.
value_semantics: 0.0 (dark purple, approx RGB [20,0,40]) = minimum average rainfall; 1.0 (yellow, approx RGB [253,231,37]) = maximum average rainfall. No units labelled. Pixel luminance mean ~67/255 indicates most of the planet is relatively dry; the equatorial band concentrates the high-rainfall signal. The minimum-valued region (~1% of pixels at the darkest purple) likely represents extreme rain-shadow or polar desert.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, exact 2:1 ratio, matches the standard Gleba export resolution
integration_notes: This is a direct fit for Project-R's RAINFALL MAP slot (per-node runoff weighting for stream-power erosion). Integration steps: (1) At load time, decode the viridis ramp to a float32 single-channel array using the nearest-LUT-entry method above; store as a (2048,4096) array in [0,1]. (2) When a section is selected, crop and reproject the decoded array into the oblique Hammer section exactly as the heightmap is handled — resampling is fine since rainfall is a smooth field. (3) Pass the resampled scalar grid as the `rainfall` weight array into the erosion node; it scales local runoff accumulation (higher weight -> more incision). No further normalisation is needed unless the erosion code expects mm/yr — in that case multiply by a user-supplied max_rainfall_mm_yr parameter. The viridis-to-scalar decode should be done once on load, not per-section, to avoid repeated LUT operations.
caveats: 1. Viridis 8-bit encoding caps precision at 256 discrete rainfall levels; fine for erosion weighting but not for scientific quantification. 2. No physical units are embedded — only relative intensity is recoverable without a companion legend or metadata file. 3. Likely accompanied by MinRainfall.png and MaxRainfall.png siblings in the same export directory; AverageRainfall is the best single map for erosion but seasonal extremes (MinRainfall for drought, MaxRainfall for flood-pulse incision) could also be wired in. Check for those before finalising the rainfall slot. 4. The dark-purple ocean areas may encode near-zero rainfall over sea surface — verify that the land/sea mask from a sibling map is used to exclude ocean pixels so they do not suppress runoff at coastal cells.

name: Biome
represents: Discrete biome / land-cover classes across the planet surface, with ocean areas left as white (no biome assigned). 13 unique flat-fill colors covering approximately 12 land biome classes plus an implicit ocean class (white).
decode_recipe: All 13 colors are exact 8-bit flat fills — no anti-aliasing between classes. Build a 13-entry palette lookup table and map each pixel to its nearest entry (exact match works for most pixels; use nearest-L2 in RGB space for any boundary bleed pixels). Palette and tentative class labels: [255,255,255]=ocean/null (77.1%), [255,246,213]=arid desert/bare (7.0%), [205,222,135]=light grassland/shrub (5.0%), [113,200,55]=open forest/grass (1.9%), [135,222,205]=teal coastal wetland or shallow water (1.7%), [68,120,33]=mixed forest (1.4%), [236,236,236]=polar/ice/tundra (1.4%), [0,85,0]=dense jungle (1.4%), [44,160,90]=tropical/medium forest (1.3%), [255,221,85]=steppe/dry grassland (0.8%), [212,170,0]=savanna/golden grassland (0.8%), [200,113,55]=desert scrub/laterite (0.3%), plus one additional color below 0.1% not captured in top-12. Class labels are inferred from color appearance; verify against Gleba generator's biome enum. Output: integer class raster [0..12].
value_semantics: Each pixel value is a discrete biome class ID with no ordinal meaning. White [255,255,255] is the null/ocean class. No physical units. No colorbar present in the image — class names must be cross-referenced against the Gleba planet generator's biome definitions.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (standard Gleba export resolution, confirmed 2:1 aspect)
integration_notes: Three uses: (1) world_map slot — load as-is in sRGB; visually readable on the preview sphere but 77% ocean white makes it less attractive than a TrueColor or shaded-relief composite. (2) section_selection overlay — render as a tinted categorical layer on the sphere so the user can click into a specific biome zone (e.g. dense jungle, coastal wetland). Requires a small palette-to-color UI legend. (3) Derived land_sea_mask — threshold: pixels where all channels == 255 → 0 (ocean), else → 1 (land). This gives Project-R a precise coastline mask at full resolution for free, without a separate mask export. For a future erodibility extension, a coarse biome-to-K_sp table (e.g. bare rock > desert > grassland > forest) could drive spatial K_sp from the class raster, but this is speculative and would need tuning against real lithology.
caveats: Ocean is encoded as pure white [255,255,255] rather than a separate channel or alpha, so any land pixel that happens to be near-white (polar ice at [236,236,236]) is close to the null color — ensure the land/sea mask uses exact equality on all three channels, not a luminance threshold. Biome class names are not embedded in the image; the color-to-name mapping depends entirely on the Gleba generator's internal biome enum and may differ between generator versions. At 77% ocean coverage most of the raster is uninformative for land erosion workflows. If a separate LandSeaMask.png exists in the export set, prefer it over deriving one from this map. The 13th color not appearing in the top-12 list has negligible coverage (less than 0.05%) and may be an artefact of boundary bleed between adjacent biomes during export.

name: ClimateContinentality
represents: Climate continentality index — how far each land location is from maritime/oceanic influence; proxy for seasonal temperature extremes and aridity of the continental interior
decode_recipe: Ocean fill is RGB(30,30,30) — mask these out first (abs(R-30)<8 AND G==B==R). For land pixels the ramp is a custom 3-stop encoding: low continentality = blue (0,0,255), mid = magenta (255,0,255), high = white (255,255,255). No standard matplotlib colormap fits (all mean_err > 0.16). Best scalar approximation without the source LUT: normalize per channel — continentality_01 ≈ clamp((R + G - B + 255) / 510, 0, 1), which yields ~0 for pure blue (maritime coast) and ~1 for white (deep interior). Green channel is near-zero across most of the range and only rises to 255 at the white (maximum) pole, so it can be ignored except as a saturation flag. Treat the result as a relative index [0,1]; no physical unit range is visible in the image.
value_semantics: Black/dark-grey (30,30,30) = ocean no-data. Blue = low continentality (maritime/coastal). Magenta/fuchsia = moderate-high continentality. White = maximum continentality (deep continental interior). No legend or numeric range is embedded in the image; units are dimensionless [0,1] relative to the planet's own range.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), same footprint as the other Gleba exports
integration_notes: No direct slot in the current Project-R pipeline. Two potential uses: (1) Section-selection guidance — high-continentality regions correlate with arid interiors where wind/flash-flood erosion dominates over river incision; expose as a heatmap overlay on the preview sphere so the user can consciously pick maritime vs continental sections. (2) Future K_sp / erodibility driver — continental interiors tend to be drier, less vegetated, and more erodible by flash events but less by sustained runoff; a mapped continentality field could modulate K_sp spatially if Project-R ever supports that. Neither use requires more than the approximate scalar decode above. To load: decode via the channel formula above, write to a float32 grayscale array, mask ocean to NaN, resample to section resolution.
caveats: Ocean fill is RGB(30,30,30) not true black — a naive grayscale luminance threshold will misclassify it as low-continentality land; always mask explicitly. The custom colormap cannot be inverted with a named matplotlib LUT, so the scalar decode is an approximation; if the Gleba generator source exposes a palette table, prefer that. This map carries no erosion physics on its own — it is a climate descriptor, not a process rate. Potential redundancy with ClimatePrecipitation and ClimateTemperature maps in the export set, which together already imply continentality; this map is a derived summary of those.

name: ClimateLandVsSea
represents: Binary land / sea mask — white = land, black = ocean
decode_recipe: Convert to single channel: take R (== G == B). The result is a near-binary mask: values ~255 = land, values ~0 = sea, with a thin band of anti-aliased gray at coastlines. To get a clean boolean mask: pixel >= 128 → land (1), else sea (0). For a soft coastal weight (e.g. to taper erosion near shore), normalise: weight = R / 255.0. No colormap inversion needed — scalar is luminance directly.
value_semantics: Black (0) = ocean / sea, covering ~73.6% of pixels. White (255) = land, covering ~20.9% of pixels. Remaining ~5.5% are anti-aliased coastline fringe values 1–254. No physical units; purely topological.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, 2:1 aspect, matches the standard Gleba export resolution
integration_notes: Slot: land_sea_mask input (extension opportunity — Project-R does not yet have an explicit mask slot). Decode on load: single-channel float32, R/255. Use the threshold (>=0.5) mask to: (1) restrict stream-power erosion to land pixels only, avoiding artefacts where the heightmap dips below sea level near coasts; (2) drive the coastal/wave erosion pass — the coastline boundary is the set of land pixels adjacent to sea pixels; (3) define the ocean fill level for the continental-shelf blending pass more precisely than a raw brightness threshold on the heightmap. If Project-R already derives land/sea from the heightmap via a brightness cutoff, this map offers a cross-check / authoritative override. Priority for implementation: coastal erosion stage, which currently needs to detect the shoreline from the heightmap alone.
caveats: Redundant with any heightmap-derived land/sea threshold; if TileElevation* maps encode ocean as black and land as positive, this mask adds little for simple cases. Its value is mainly for planets where the elevation-to-sea-level relationship is ambiguous or where the generator's sea level is not at elevation=0. The "Climate" prefix in the name suggests this may reflect a climate-model sea level (e.g. ice-age variant with lower sea level) rather than purely topographic land — check against sibling maps (e.g. any "NoIce" vs default variant) if ice-age and modern variants exist in the export. Anti-aliased coast fringe may produce a 1–2 pixel border of partial land weight; threshold at 0.5 cleanly removes it.

name: ClimateOceanCurrents
represents: Ocean current climate zone categories across the planet surface, with landmasses shown in neutral gray. Encodes discrete current-type or climate-zone classes (cold polar, warm tropical, intermediate) via a small fixed-color palette.
decode_recipe: Only ~5-7 truly distinct palette entries exist; the 69 unique colors are the base classes plus anti-aliasing interpolation at zone edges. Nearest-RGB-distance assignment: build a palette table from the dominant colors and snap every pixel to its closest entry. Approximate palette: land = [80,80,80], cold-polar = [38,41,49], warm-tropical-ocean = [69,65,49], and 2-4 intermediate zone tones around [65-70, 62-66, 48-50]. For any downstream use, clamp edge pixels (those not matching any base class within a tolerance of ~5 RGB counts) to their nearest base class.
value_semantics: Purely categorical; no physical scalar, no units, no legend or colorbar visible in the image. Color identity encodes ocean current zone type (cold/warm/polar/equatorial etc.). Land appears as mid-gray [80,80,80] covering ~23% of pixels. Ocean zones span luminance ~40-50 (cold dark navy-gray polar bands top and bottom) to ~60-70 (olive warm tropical mid-latitudes).
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), pixel-aligned with the sibling heightmap exports
integration_notes: No current Project-R erosion slot maps to ocean current zones. Could be draped on the preview sphere as a world_map layer but the palette is very dark and muted (luminance 40-80/255) making it a poor visual display; the TileColor or surface-texture export will be far more useful for that role. As an extension, the cold-polar vs warm-tropical zone mask could weakly proxy a coastal erosion intensity modifier (cold polar = ice/wave energy) but this would require game-data research to confirm semantics before wiring. Most practical use is informational reference during section selection to identify coastlines with interesting current exposure.
caveats: Class semantics (which color = which current type) are not labeled in the image and require cross-referencing Gleba game data or documentation. The 69 unique colors are mostly anti-aliasing noise at zone boundaries, not 69 distinct classes. Palette is extremely dark and low-contrast — unsuitable as a standalone world map display. Redundant with other climate exports (e.g. ClimatePrecipitation, wind maps) that directly drive erosion-relevant quantities like rainfall; this map adds no unique erosion-driving signal those others do not already cover.

name: ClimateSurfaceWinds
represents: Global surface wind speed (or wind intensity index) encoded as a smooth spatial field, with wind direction streamlines/arrows overlaid as red-orange pixel traces along coastlines and convergence zones
decode_recipe: 1. Build the matplotlib cividis LUT: `import matplotlib.cm as cm; lut = (cm.cividis(np.linspace(0,1,256))[:,:3]*255).astype(np.uint8)`. 2. For each pixel, compute squared RGB distance to all 256 LUT entries; take argmin -> index in [0,255]. 3. Normalize: scalar = index / 255.0, giving [0,1] where 0=dark blue (low wind) and 1=bright yellow (high wind). 4. MASK OUT the overlaid streamline/arrow pixels before decoding: identify pixels whose RGB does not match any cividis entry within a threshold (e.g. nearest-LUT mean_err > 0.08 per channel); these red-orange and violet-blue traces are direction indicators, not wind speed data, and should be excluded or inpainted from neighbors. Physical units are unknown (no legend present); treat as a relative wind intensity field unless a companion metadata file supplies m/s range.
value_semantics: Dark navy blue = minimum wind speed (poles and calm zones, luminance ~31/255); bright yellow = maximum wind speed (mid-latitude westerlies/trade-wind belts, luminance ~198/255). Value range in cividis index space is roughly 0.0 to 1.0 relative. No colorbar or numeric legend is visible in the image. The red-orange and blue-violet streaks on and near coastlines are overlaid wind direction arrows, not wind-speed values.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), standard Gleba export resolution, pixel-aligned with the heightmap exports
integration_notes: No current Project-R slot accepts wind data. Do not wire into rainfall, heightmap, or bathymetry slots. Potential extension: a coastal-erosion intensity pass could weight wave energy by prevailing onshore wind magnitude — load via decode recipe above, crop/reproject alongside the heightmap section, then multiply the coastal erosion K factor by the resampled wind scalar at each coastal pixel. This requires implementing a new "wind" input slot in the coastal erosion operator. For now, the image can be loaded as the World Map display texture only if the wind-direction overlays (which discolor large coastal stretches) are acceptable for visualization; otherwise it is aesthetically distracting compared to a true color world map.
caveats: 1. Overlaid wind-direction streamlines (red-orange and blue-violet jagged traces concentrated on coastlines and jet-stream zones) are rendered on top of the cividis ramp; these pixels will yield garbage on colormap inversion and must be masked before any numerical use. 2. Physical units (m/s or dimensionless index) are not recoverable from the image alone — no legend visible. 3. Surface wind is not precipitation: this map cannot substitute for the rainfall map as an erosion driver without a separate wind-to-precipitation model. 4. No sibling wind maps were observed in the export set to cross-check against; verify whether an upper-level or seasonal variant exists before discarding.

name: CombinedTectonics
represents: Global tectonic scalar field (likely uplift rate or crustal stress) encoded in viridis colormap, with tectonic plate boundary lines baked in as colored overlays (blue = divergent/spreading, dark-red = convergent/subduction, green = transform or other type)
decode_recipe: 1. Build matplotlib viridis LUT: `lut = plt.get_cmap('viridis')(np.linspace(0,1,256))[:,:3]` (256x3, float32).  2. Load image as uint8 RGB array (H,W,3).  3. Create a boundary-line mask: flag pixels whose RGB is near (0,0,150) blue, (100,0,0) dark-red, or (0,128,0) green within Euclidean distance 30 — these are plate-boundary lines baked in; set scalar to NaN for those pixels.  4. Flag the solid-gray fill (80,80,80) ± 5 — these represent ocean/stable-plate no-data regions; set scalar to 0 or NaN depending on use.  5. For remaining pixels: compute squared Euclidean distance from pixel RGB to each of the 256 LUT entries (scaled to 0-255); take argmin → index in [0,255]; scalar = index/255 in [0,1].  6. Rescale scalar to physical units if a legend is available (none visible in this export — treat [0,1] as relative tectonic intensity until calibrated).  Note: viridis runs dark-purple (low) → blue/teal → green → yellow (high); the visible image shows mostly green-to-yellow range, meaning the planet's active land is in the mid-to-high tectonic intensity band.
value_semantics: 0 (dark purple/black in viridis) = minimum tectonic intensity; 1 (yellow) = maximum. No numeric legend visible in the export — units unknown, treat as normalized [0,1] relative uplift/stress. The gray fill (RGB 80,80,80, ~22.7% of pixels) is a flat fill for ocean plates or stable cratons — not part of the viridis ramp. Plate boundary line pixels (~thin 1-2px strokes) are corrupted and carry no scalar meaning.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), matches the standard Gleba export resolution
integration_notes: Primary use: spatial UPLIFT field U for the erosion extension. After decode, pass the [0,1] scalar grid as a per-pixel uplift multiplier into the stream-power stage (U_local = U_base * scalar). Steps to wire in: (1) on manifest load, decode viridis → scalar using the recipe above, store as float32 single-channel; (2) crop+reproject the scalar section alongside the heightmap section; (3) in erosion.py multiply the stream-power uplift term by the local scalar. The gray ocean fill should be zeroed out (ocean does not uplift). The baked boundary lines (thin 1-2px) are best healed by a 3x3 median inpaint over the masked pixels before use as a spatial field. Secondary use: world-map display layer — the viridis + colored boundary lines makes a visually distinctive sphere texture, usable as-is in the WORLD MAP slot.
caveats: 1. Boundary lines are baked into the raster — they corrupt thin strips of scalar data and must be masked and inpainted before use as a clean uplift field. 2. 8-bit only (429 unique colors after the gray fill and line colors are excluded) — viridis ramp is effectively 8-bit quantized, producing mild banding in the uplift field; no 16-bit version available. 3. Physical units unknown — no legend/colorbar in the export; the [0,1] scalar is relative only. 4. The gray fill (80,80,80) occupies 22.7% of pixels (ocean/stable plates) and sits outside the viridis ramp — needs explicit handling to avoid being mapped to a spurious scalar value (nearest viridis match for that gray would be around index 70/255, which is incorrect). 5. Redundancy: if a companion TectonicStress or UpliftRate single-channel map exists in the export set, prefer that over this composite. Check sibling exports for a cleaner scalar-only tectonic map before routing this through the viridis decode pipeline.

name: CrustMap
represents: Binary continental-crust mask: white = continental crust, black = oceanic crust / ocean basin. Marks tectonic crust type, not strictly land vs. sea (shallow continental shelves may appear white even if below sea level).
channels_bitdepth: 3ch 8-bit RGB (all three channels identical), 4096x2048. Only 2 unique values: 0 and 255.
decode_recipe: Convert to single-channel L: `mask = np.array(Image.open(path).convert('L'))`. Threshold: pixels == 255 → continental crust (1); pixels == 0 → oceanic crust / ocean (0). No LUT, no colormap, no interpolation needed. Result is a boolean uint8 array of shape (2048, 4096).
value_semantics: Black (0) = 74.84% of pixels = oceanic crust / ocean. White (255) = 25.16% of pixels = continental crust / landmass. No intermediate values exist. No physical units; it is a categorical crust-type flag.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1 aspect), matches the standard Gleba export resolution used by the sibling maps.
integration_notes: Primary use: land/sea mask slot. Load as a uint8 binary array and use it to set ocean pixels to a fixed base elevation (e.g. 0 m) before erosion, rather than relying on a brightness threshold on the heightmap. This gives a clean, unambiguous shoreline definition. Secondary extension use: feed as a spatial erodibility modifier K_sp — continental crust could carry a different base erodibility than oceanic crust if the simulation ever extends into partially-submerged coastal zones. Not suited for rainfall, bathymetry, or world-map display roles.
caveats: Crust type != land surface: continental crust includes shallow shelves that may still be below sea level in the heightmap, so the mask boundary will not align perfectly with the shoreline visible in the elevation data. Cross-check against TileElevation or the heightmap before using as a sea-level mask. 8-bit storage is fine given binary content (no banding risk). No legend or colorbar present in the image — interpretation of white=continental is inferred from name and visual shape matching the Gleba landmasses.

name: DebugIsLand
represents: Binary land/sea mask — pixels mark whether each cell is land (island) or ocean
channels_bitdepth: 3ch 8-bit RGB (all three channels identical), 4096x2048 — effectively 1-bit data stored in an 8-bit RGB file
decode_recipe: Read any single channel (R, G, or B are identical). Two values only: 30 = ocean, 80 = land. Threshold at midpoint: pixel_value >= 55 → land (1), else ocean (0). No colormap involved; no LUT needed. Result is a boolean mask array of shape (2048, 4096).
value_semantics: Value 30 (~77% of pixels) = ocean/sea. Value 80 (~23% of pixels) = land. No physical units; no legend present. The specific grey levels (30, 80) appear to be internal Gleba generator debug output values with no physical meaning beyond the binary distinction.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), matches the standard Gleba export resolution
integration_notes: As a land_sea_mask: load the R channel, threshold at 55, pass the boolean array into Project-R's sea-level/ocean definition so the erosion pipeline knows the precise coastline without relying on a brightness threshold of the heightmap. This is useful for coastal erosion passes (wave erosion stage) and for preventing river routing from crossing into sea cells. As section_selection guidance: overlay the mask on the preview sphere so the user can visually pick land regions — useful because landmasses are scattered and small (~23% coverage). Implementation: on load, binarise (>= 55) and cache as a uint8 mask; apply same equirect-to-oblique-Hammer crop as the heightmap so both arrays stay pixel-aligned.
caveats: Potentially redundant with a sea-level threshold on the heightmap (TileElevation or equivalent) — if that map has a clear sea-level value, this mask adds little. Verify whether the heightmap already encodes a flat ocean floor at a fixed elevation before adding this as a separate input. The two stored grey levels (30, 80) have no meaning beyond land/sea; do not attempt to read sub-levels or intermediate values from this file. Stored as 3-channel RGB despite being 1-bit data — wasteful but harmless; convert to single-channel bool on load to save memory.

name: ErosionTimeWaterflow
represents: Accumulated waterflow / drainage flux across land surfaces, color-coded with viridis; bright yellow-green threads are major river channels, dark purple is low-flow land, near-black is ocean (no-data sentinel)
decode_recipe: 1. Ocean/no-data mask: pixels where R<35 AND G<35 AND B<35 (dominant color (30,30,30) is ~77% of image) → set scalar to NaN / skip. 2. For remaining land pixels: build the matplotlib viridis LUT at 256 entries (call matplotlib.colormaps['viridis'](np.linspace(0,1,256)) and convert to uint8 RGB). 3. For each land pixel, find the nearest LUT entry by Euclidean distance in RGB space → that entry's index / 255 gives a normalized scalar in [0, 1]. 4. scalar=0 is viridis dark-purple (low accumulated flow); scalar=1 is viridis yellow (high flow / major rivers). No absolute physical units are visible; the range is relative within each planet export. Note: the analyzer's cmap_fit ranked cubehelix first only because the (30,30,30) background sentinel dominates the fit; the actual land palette is clearly viridis (purple→blue→cyan→yellow progression matches viridis exactly).
value_semantics: Relative waterflow accumulation index, [0,1] after LUT inversion. Low values (purple) = minimal drainage / arid interior / high ground with short flow paths. High values (yellow) = major trunk rivers with large upstream catchments. No legend or physical units visible in the image. Ocean background sentinel is (30,30,30), not pure black.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, confirmed 2:1 aspect ratio, pixel-aligned with the other Gleba exports
integration_notes: Primary use in Project-R is limited because Project-R already derives its own flow accumulation from the heightmap during the stream-power erosion pass — importing the planet generator's pre-computed flow would be circular. Two narrow legitimate uses: (1) LAND/SEA MASK: threshold the (30,30,30) sentinel to get a binary ocean mask without needing a separate mask layer — load image, apply `np.all(arr < 35, axis=-1)` → ocean pixels; feed into the coastline/continental-shelf pass as a hard ocean boundary. (2) DISPLAY: overlay the viridis ramp on the preview sphere as an informational layer showing the source planet's drainage topology; useful for the user to orient section selection around major river basins. As a RAINFALL MAP input it would be wrong — this is accumulated flow (a downstream integral), not input precipitation rate; using it as rainfall would double-count flow and produce unrealistic incision. If Project-R later gains a flow-network seeding extension, the river-channel pixels (scalar > 0.85, bright yellow) could initialize trunk channel positions before the erosion solver runs.
caveats: The map encodes a derived erosion output (flow accumulation), not a primary physical field, so it carries no unique information beyond what a correctly run stream-power model on the heightmap would regenerate. name: ErosionTimeWaterflowCutoff

  (68,  1, 84)   → class 1 = land, below cutoff     (21.2 %)
  (254,231, 36)  → class 2 = river channel, above cutoff (1.7 %)

Class 2 = land where waterflow exceeds the cutoff, forming the active drainage / river network skeleton (viridis yellow branching lines). No legend or unit annotation visible.

(1) Land/sea mask extension: class 0 pixels give a clean binary ocean mask — if Project-R ever adds an explicit land/sea-mask slot, this delivers it precisely (OR with the black pixels from TileElevation* or similar). name: GeographicArea
represents: Per-cell geographic area weight on the spherical planet — an equirectangular correction factor used by the planet generator to account for how much physical surface area each grid cell represents. Dark (near-black) pixels mark ocean / zero-area cells; bright white pixels mark land cells with high physical area (largest near the equator). Not a terrain property like elevation or rainfall.
decode_recipe: Extract luminance: L = (R*0.299 + G*0.587 + B*0.114) / 255. No clean colormap was identified (best cmap fit cubehelix mean_err=0.077, ramp_coverage=31% — too poor to use LUT inversion). The scalar field is L directly. To extract a land/sea mask: threshold at L > ~0.15 (empirically, the ocean cluster peaks near lum bucket 1-2 / L≈0.05 and land peaks at lum buckets 9-12 / L≈0.35–0.55). Color noise on land (slight R/G/B variation around a dark-blue base of B≈50) is irrelevant noise; discard chroma and use luminance only.
value_semantics: Black / near-black (RGB ≈ [20, 20, 50]) = ocean or pole cells with negligible physical area. Bright white (RGB ≈ [200, 200, 200+]) = land cells with maximum geographic area. Value min≈14.6, max≈198.5, mean≈59.3 (luminance in 0–255 range). No legend or colorbar visible; no physical units (it is a dimensionless weighting factor).
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, 2:1 aspect confirmed
integration_notes: Only plausible use in Project-R is as a rough land/sea mask: threshold luminance at ~0.15, binarize to land=1/ocean=0, and feed into the coastline/land-sea mask extension slot. However, the heightmap already encodes land vs. sea implicitly (ocean = low brightness / near zero), so this map is redundant in any setup that includes the heightmap. Do not use as heightmap, rainfall, or bathymetry — it carries no elevation or hydrological signal. If a clean land/sea mask is needed, prefer deriving it from the heightmap's zero-level threshold rather than this map.

This is almost certainly an internal planet-generator correction factor (geographic area per equirectangular cell), not a terrain property — its primary use in the generator is resource distribution weighting, not visualization. 2. Redundant with the land/sea boundary already implicit in the heightmap and in any TileElevation sibling. 3. 8-bit with noticeable RGB color noise on land (B channel pinned at ≈50 in ocean, uncorrelated R/G variation on land) makes precise threshold extraction slightly noisy; apply a small median blur before thresholding. 4. No physical range or units are recoverable — no legend present.

No standard colormap LUT applies — colors are arbitrary per-region palette entries. 3. OUTPUT: integer label image (0=ocean, 1..N=region ID). name: GeologicProvince
represents: Discrete tectonic/geologic province classes: oceanic crust, continental craton, passive margin/shelf, elevated shield, and active orogenic belt / volcanic arc
decode_recipe:
Exactly 5 discrete colors — map each pixel to its class by nearest-color match (Euclidean distance in RGB):
  (50,  50,  50)  → class 0: oceanic crust / ocean basin  (37.3% of map)
  (136, 153, 170) → class 1: continental craton            (58.6%)
  (170, 187, 204) → class 2: passive margin / shelf        ( 0.9%)
  (204, 221, 238) → class 3: elevated shield               ( 0.6%)
  (153, 255, 204) → class 4: active orogen / volcanic arc  ( 2.6%)
No interpolation; assign by nearest palette entry only. For K_sp driver: map class→float, e.g. {0:NaN, 1:0.2, 2:0.5, 3:0.3, 4:1.0} (relative softness, tune to taste). For uplift driver: {0:0, 1:0.1, 2:0.05, 3:0.15, 4:1.0} (relative U, normalized). For land/sea mask: class 0 = sea, classes 1-4 = land (binary).
value_semantics: No physical units — purely categorical. Class 4 (bright cyan #99FFCC) marks active convergent/divergent plate boundaries and volcanic arcs as continuous linear belts. Class 0 (near-black #323232) is the ocean floor. Classes 1-3 are shades of blue-gray distinguishing craton from margin from shield. No legend or colorbar present in the image; classes inferred from visual topology and color identity.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, exactly 2:1, pixel-aligned with the standard Gleba export resolution

(1) Spatial erodibility K_sp: after class-decode, bilinearly resample to section resolution and multiply the base K_sp scalar by the per-pixel factor — class 4 (volcanic arc) should be softest, class 1 (craton) hardest. (2) Spatial uplift U: same decode path; class 4 belts get highest U, driving mountain-building in the erosion ODE. (3) Land/sea mask: class 0 = ocean gives a crisp alternative to the brightness-threshold approach currently used on the heightmap — useful for defining sea level without tuning a threshold. (4) Section selection guidance: the bright cyan volcanic arc belts are visually striking and geologically rich targets; a helper that highlights class-4 pixels on the preview sphere would steer users toward interesting sections. Wire-in order of priority: land/sea mask first (zero-cost, high value), then K_sp, then U.

The oceanic-crust class (class 0) covers 37% of the map but is irrelevant to land erosion; always mask it out before computing drainage stats. Thin boundary pixels between provinces may not cleanly snap to any of the 5 palette entries if anti-aliasing was applied at export — nearest-color matching handles this correctly. No ice-age vs. no-ice variant distinction applies here (geology is static). Check against TectonicPlate and CrustType sibling exports if present — they may encode overlapping information at different granularity.

name: InAndOutFlow
represents: Net hydraulic flow balance per land cell — a diverging scalar encoding inflow-dominant (basin/sink) vs outflow-dominant (upland/source) zones, with river/watershed-boundary lines overlaid in yellow-green. Black is ocean/no-data.
decode_recipe:
Three visually distinct classes dominate (159 total unique colors): (1) Black/near-black (30,30,30) ~77% — ocean / null, zero-flow mask. (2) Purple (~77,60,81) ~9.4% — net-inflow / convergence zones (basins, valley floors, lowlands). (3) Blue-gray/teal (~72,84,95 and neighbours) ~22% — net-outflow / divergence zones (uplands, slopes draining away). (4) Yellow-green lines (~180,200,60 range, sparse) — river channels or watershed divide boundaries.

No standard matplotlib colormap fits (best cubehelix at mean_err 0.10, only 34% coverage). This is a custom Gleba engine palette, not a recoverable scientific ramp.

To extract a scalar: threshold by hue. Convert to HSV. Pixels with V < 0.15 → class 0 (ocean). Remaining pixels: H in 270–320° (purple) → class 1 (inflow); H in 180–230° (teal-blue) → class 2 (outflow); H in 60–90° (yellow-green) → class 3 (river lines). A signed scalar can be approximated as: value = (R − B) / 255, giving negative for teal outflow and positive for purple inflow, with ~0 for the ocean mask after excluding V < 0.15.
value_semantics: Black = ocean / no data. Purple = net inflow (water accumulates; basins, lowlands). Teal-gray = net outflow (water drains away; uplands, ridges). Yellow-green lines = river channels or watershed divides. No physical units or legend visible. Raw pixel range 30–113 in 8-bit luminance; actual scalar range is not quantified in absolute terms.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), standard Gleba export resolution matching the heightmap
integration_notes: Project-R generates its own drainage network from the heightmap via stream-power erosion, so this map does not add new information to the erosion pipeline itself. Two narrow uses: (1) Section selection guidance — the purple inflow basins highlight the geomorphologically active lowland zones most likely to produce interesting erosion; displaying this on the preview sphere alongside the world map could help users pick productive sections. (2) Display-only overlay on the sphere to visualise catchment structure. Do NOT feed this as a rainfall or erodibility driver — the diverging encoding (inflow vs outflow) does not correspond to precipitation intensity. If a future extension adds watershed-aware K_sp variation, the inflow/outflow split could seed that, but decoding is manual (HSV thresholding above).

The yellow-green river lines are very sparse and thin (single-pixel in places) and will alias badly at section crop resolution. The encoding is a custom Gleba palette with no documented standard; the HSV decode recipe above is a reverse-engineering approximation. 77% of the image is the constant near-black ocean fill, so land-area statistics occupy only ~23% of pixels. Redundancy: if a TileElevation or land-sea mask is available in the same export, the ocean mask here adds nothing. The inflow/outflow pattern is largely derivable from the heightmap itself by Project-R's own flow routing, making this map genuinely redundant for the erosion workflow.

name: JanuaryRainfall
represents: Monthly precipitation (January) across the planet surface — relative rainfall intensity showing ITCZ/monsoon belt and dry continental/polar regions
decode_recipe: 1. Build the matplotlib viridis LUT: `import matplotlib.cm as cm; lut = (cm.get_cmap('viridis', 256)(range(256))[:, :3] * 255).astype(uint8)` — gives a (256,3) uint8 array. 2. For each pixel (r,g,b), find the nearest LUT entry by minimum Euclidean distance in RGB space: `idx = argmin(sum((lut - [r,g,b])**2, axis=1))`. 3. Normalized rainfall = idx / 255.0, range [0, 1] where 0 = driest and 1 = wettest. 4. Physical units are not shown (no legend/colorbar in image); scale by known max from Gleba documentation if available, otherwise use the [0,1] scalar directly as a relative runoff weight. The analyzer confirms viridis with mean_err=0.036 and ramp_coverage=1.0 — fit is reliable.
value_semantics: Black/dark purple (viridis index ~0, ~2.2% of pixels at minimum value 10.5) = near-zero rainfall / arid zones. Yellow (viridis index ~255, value_max 215.6) = maximum precipitation, concentrated in a bright equatorial ITCZ-like band. Mean luminance ~66/255 (~index 80) indicates a predominantly dry planet with a narrow high-rainfall belt. No physical units (mm/day or mm/month) are recoverable from the image alone.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, exact 2:1 aspect ratio, matches the standard Gleba export resolution
integration_notes: Slot directly into Project-R's RAINFALL MAP input after decoding viridis index to [0,1]. The decode step must happen on load (not at erosion time) since Project-R expects a single-channel float or grayscale image: convert to a 4096x2048 float32 array of normalized indices, then save as a 16-bit grayscale PNG (multiply by 65535) for lossless resampling. At section crop time, Project-R bilinearly resamples this to the section resolution — the continuous viridis ramp survives resampling cleanly. January-specific data means erosion driven by this map models northern-hemisphere winter runoff; for a year-round average, blend with the companion JulyRainfall map (weight 0.5 each) or use an annual mean map if present in the export. Check the export folder for JulyRainfall.png and AnnualRainfall.png before choosing which to load.

No colorbar is embedded, so the absolute rainfall scale (mm/day or mm/month) is unknown — the [0,1] relative scalar is sufficient for stream-power weighting but prevents physically calibrated discharge estimates. 8-bit colormap encoding introduces quantization: only 256 discrete rainfall levels are representable, and viridis index retrieval via nearest-color adds a small additional error (mean 0.036 in RGB space). The pronounced polar darkness (near-zero rainfall at poles) is physically reasonable but may over-suppress any polar erosion pass.

name: JulyRainfall

Pattern is climatologically coherent for a July summer monsoon configuration.

For each pixel RGB, find nearest LUT entry by minimizing squared Euclidean distance across all 256 entries. 3. The result is a scalar index in [0, 255]; divide by 255 to get normalized rainfall in [0, 1]. 4. If physical units are needed and a reference range is supplied externally (e.g. 0–500 mm/month from the Gleba export metadata), multiply by that range. No legend is embedded in the image so units cannot be recovered from pixels alone. The viridis fit is very strong (mean_err 0.036, ramp_coverage 1.0, confirmed by viridis endpoints: dark purple (20,0,40) at index ~0 and bright yellow (254,231,36) at index ~255 both present in top_colors).

Viridis index 255 (bright yellow, RGB ~254,231,36) = maximum rainfall (~3.2% of pixels, equatorial ITCZ core). Mid-range blue-purple (~65,65,134) dominates the subtropical and polar regions. No physical unit range is visible in the image; normalized [0,1] is usable as-is for relative runoff weighting.

integration_notes: Direct drop-in for Project-R's RAINFALL MAP slot. After viridis decode to [0,1] scalar, pass the cropped section tile as the per-node runoff multiplier in the stream-power erosion stage. The equatorial ITCZ band will concentrate incision at low latitudes, which is physically correct. Resample to section resolution on load (bilinear is fine; rainfall is smooth). No masking needed — ocean pixels will have non-zero viridis-decoded values but the heightmap's sea-level mask will suppress erosion there regardless. No physical range (mm/month) is embedded — check Gleba export metadata or companion documentation to rescale. name: Koppen

decode_recipe: Build a fixed palette LUT of all 28 observed RGB values and map each to a Koppen class label. Key entries from the analyzer: (255,255,255)=Ocean, (255,0,0)=hot arid/BWh or Aw tropical savanna, (255,150,150)=BSh hot steppe, (178,178,178)=gray polar/tundra ET, (0,126,126)=dark teal subarctic Dfc, (245,163,0)=orange BSk/semi-arid, (104,104,104)=mid-gray EF ice cap, (255,219,99)=yellow Csa/subtropical dry, (56,199,255)=light blue Cfb/oceanic, (70,169,255)=steel blue Dfb/humid continental, (198,1,199)=magenta Cwa/Am monsoon, (90,119,219)=slate-blue Dfc/Dwc. For boundary pixels with intermediate colors not in the palette, assign nearest-color by Euclidean RGB distance. Result is a per-pixel class integer (0=ocean, 1..N=land climate class). No scalar inversion needed; this is a label map only.
value_semantics: 28 discrete classes; 77.1% of pixels are white (ocean/no class). Remaining ~23% land pixels cover the full Koppen hierarchy A (tropical), B (arid/semi-arid), C (temperate), D (continental/boreal), E (polar). No physical magnitude is encoded — classes are nominal, not ordinal. No legend is visible in the image file itself; class-to-color mapping must be sourced from the Gleba planet generator's Koppen palette documentation.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), matches the standard Gleba export resolution; pixel-aligned with heightmap
integration_notes: Not usable as a heightmap, rainfall, or bathymetry input — it is purely a climate-class label map. Two concrete uses: (1) Display-only: load as the world_map slot on the preview sphere so the user sees biome regions when selecting a section — the bright palette is visually distinctive and aids section picking. (2) Section-selection guidance: a user wanting to erode a hot-arid (red) vs boreal (teal) landscape can visually target those zones. Extension opportunity: the Koppen A-group (tropical) implies high rainfall; B-group implies low rainfall. A thin adapter could translate class labels to a synthetic rainfall scalar (e.g. Af=1.0, BWh=0.05) and feed it into the rainfall slot — but this would duplicate information already present in a dedicated rainfall export if one exists in the same export set. Check for a Precipitation or Rainfall PNG in the export folder before building that adapter. No erodibility (K_sp) or uplift (U) signal is directly recoverable from climate class alone.

The 28-color palette is not the standard published Koppen RGB scheme used by Beck et al. 2018 — it is Gleba-specific, so class-to-color assignment must be confirmed from the generator's own legend or source code rather than assumed from standard Koppen color conventions. White is overloaded as ocean AND potentially as 'no data' at poles — verify polar white pixels are true ocean before using as a land/sea mask. 8-bit only, no precision concern (categorical data).

name: OldTectonicPlates
represents: Historical tectonic plate tessellation — each filled region is one ancient plate, assigned an arbitrary distinct color; ~90 plates cover the full globe with no land/sea distinction encoded.
decode_recipe: 1. Collect all unique RGB triples in the image (analyzer found 90). 2. Sort them arbitrarily and assign integer plate IDs 0..N-1 — order is irrelevant since colors carry no scalar meaning. 3. For each pixel, find its nearest entry in the 90-color palette (L2 in RGB space; exact match should suffice given hard-filled regions) and write the plate ID. Result is a uint8 plate-ID raster. Boundaries between plates are detectable by finding pixels where adjacent plate IDs differ — these are the tectonically active zones. No legend is present; color-to-plate mapping is purely nominal.
value_semantics: Each unique color = one plate ID (nominal label, no ordering, no units). Pixel value after decode = plate index 0..89. No min/max scalar range; the quantity is categorical. Plate area varies; largest plates (by pixel fraction) are ~5% of globe each.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), same resolution as the Gleba heightmap exports
integration_notes: Project-R does not yet consume categorical plate maps, but two extension paths are valuable: (1) UPLIFT field U — post-process the plate-ID raster to compute a boundary-proximity map (e.g. morphological edge detection between adjacent IDs, then distance transform inverted), giving high U near plate collisions. Wire this into the stream-power erosion stage as the spatial uplift input. (2) Section-selection guidance — highlight sections that straddle a plate boundary so the user finds tectonically interesting terrain. As a display-only world-map overlay it is vivid but uninformative to end users; prefer the color or biome map for that slot. If used for uplift, load as a categorical raster, compute the boundary mask at load time, and cache the distance-transform result alongside the section crop — do not resample categorically (use nearest-neighbor only).
