Boundary-derived uplift would therefore be an approximation at best and could misalign with actual terrain relief. No legend is present, so there is no way to recover plate names or types (oceanic vs continental) from colors alone. The analyzer's categorical_candidate flag was false due to the high color count (90), but visual inspection confirms it is unambiguously categorical. Anti-aliased edges between plates introduce a small number of mixed-color pixels that will be misclassified during nearest-color decode — apply a 1-pixel morphological closing on the ID map to clean seams before boundary detection.

name: OrogenyStrength
represents: Tectonic orogeny strength (uplift intensity) per location on the planet surface — zero over oceans/quiet cratons, grading up through active margins to bright yellow-green at active mountain belts and plate convergence zones
decode_recipe: The image is a viridis-family sequential colormap rendered at ~105 quantization levels (not a true continuous 8-bit ramp). The dominant near-black color [17,0,21] at 41.9% is a sub-viridis sentinel for ocean/zero-orogeny zones; [68,1,84] at 13.2% is viridis index ~0, the true scale minimum. Step-by-step decode: (1) Build the matplotlib viridis LUT: import matplotlib.cm as cm; lut = (cm.get_cmap("viridis")(np.linspace(0,1,256))[:,:3]*255).astype(np.uint8). (2) For each pixel, find the nearest LUT entry by Euclidean distance in RGB space -> index in [0,255]. (3) Pixels with RGB closer to [17,0,21] than to any viridis entry (L2 distance > threshold ~20) should be clamped to index 0 (ocean/zero). (4) Normalize: value = index / 255.0 -> orogeny strength in [0,1]. Bright yellow ([253,231,37]) = 1.0 = maximum orogeny; dark purple = 0.0 = inactive. No physical unit range is printed on the image; treat output as a dimensionless relative uplift factor.
value_semantics: Black/near-black [17,0,21] = zero orogeny (ocean basins, stable cratons); purple [68,1,84] = minimal but non-zero; olive/teal mid-range = moderate orogenic activity; yellow-green [70,192,110] and bright yellow = maximum active uplift. Bright yellow features are narrow curvilinear strands — clearly active mountain belts and plate convergence sutures. 42% of pixels are at the zero sentinel. No legend visible in image; value range is normalized [0,1].
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, confirmed 2:1, pixel-aligned with the other Gleba exports at the same resolution
integration_notes: This is the primary candidate for the spatial uplift field U in the stream-power erosion model (extension slot, not yet wired in Project-R). Decode to a float32 [0,1] array at load time using the viridis LUT inversion above. Feed into the erosion stage as a per-pixel U multiplier: U_eff(x,y) = U_base * orogeny_strength(x,y). Regions with high orogeny_strength will resist erosion (uplift balances incision) producing persistent mountain belts; zero-orogeny ocean pixels should be masked out before erosion (use the land/sea mask from TileElevation or a companion mask map). Because the map is already at 4096x2048, it can be cropped to the section extent in the same pass as the heightmap with no separate resampling step. The narrow yellow mountain-belt strands would also serve as useful section-selection guidance — users could pick sections centred on bright features to get geologically interesting relief.
caveats: Colormap identity is not confirmed as viridis — cmap_fit top hit is nipy_spectral (mean_err 0.091) and viridis did not appear in the top 5, possibly because the image is quantized to only 105 unique colors and ramp_coverage is low. If viridis decode produces artefacts, try inferno or magma as fallbacks (both in top 5). The near-black sentinel [17,0,21] sits outside the standard viridis range and must be handled separately or it will map to a spurious low positive value instead of zero. The 8-bit quantization (105 levels) means spatial gradients within orogenic zones are stairstepped — acceptable for a slowly varying uplift field but worth noting. Check against any sibling TectonicPlate or CrustThickness maps in the export set for redundancy before building the uplift slot.

name: PopulationDensity
represents: Spatial distribution of population density across the planet surface; land-only signal, ocean and uninhabited areas are a custom null value.
decode_recipe: 1. Mask null pixels: any pixel with RGB == [30, 30, 30] → density = 0 (these are ocean / zero-population; they are NOT part of the viridis ramp). 2. For all remaining pixels: build the matplotlib viridis LUT (256 entries × 3 uint8 via matplotlib.cm.get_cmap('viridis', 256)). Map each pixel to its nearest LUT entry by Euclidean RGB distance → that entry's index / 255 gives a normalized density in [0, 1]. Only roughly the lowest 12.5% of the viridis ramp appears (dark purple → mid purple); do not extrapolate beyond what is observed. Physical units are unknown — no legend or colorbar is present in the image; treat output as relative density [0, 1].
value_semantics: Black [30, 30, 30] = null / uninhabited (ocean or empty land). Viridis index 0 ≈ [68, 1, 84] = lowest non-zero density (4.8% of pixels). Mid-purple tones ≈ [69, 48, 124] = moderate density. No brighter greens or yellows are present, meaning the density peak is in the low end of the viridis scale. No colorbar visible; absolute units (e.g. persons/km²) are not recoverable from the image alone.
aligned_equirect: yes, 4096x2048 (2:1 aspect confirmed)
integration_notes: Load as a display-only overlay on the preview sphere to help the user pick regions of worldbuilding interest (populated continents). Do not feed it to any erosion stage — it carries no terrain, hydrology, or rock-type information. As a future extension, it could serve as a section-selection weight (bias the user's crop picker toward high-density areas) or as a post-erosion annotation layer, but neither path is currently wired in Project-R. No slot maps to it directly.
caveats: The [30, 30, 30] null value must be masked before colormap inversion — it is not viridis index 0 and will decode incorrectly if included. Only ~12% of the viridis ramp is actually used, so the recovered [0,1] values will all cluster near zero; rescaling to [min_nonzero, 1] may be more useful in practice. No physical units are visible. Luminance-based decoding will produce wrong values — nearest-LUT decode is required. No redundancy issue with other exports (population is a distinct layer), but it offers far less erosion-driving information than the climate, rainfall, or elevation maps in the same export.

name: RainShadow
represents: Rain shadow intensity — the orographic reduction in precipitation on the leeward side of terrain. High values mark the driest zones sheltered by mountain barriers; the ocean and areas with no orographic blocking are masked to a near-black sentinel.
decode_recipe:
1. Build the matplotlib viridis LUT: `lut = plt.get_cmap('viridis')(np.linspace(0,1,256))[:,:3] * 255` (256x3 uint8).
2. Identify sentinel/ocean pixels: any pixel where all three channels are near (30,30,30) — specifically where max(R,G,B) < 45. These are no-data; assign NaN or 0.
3. For all remaining land pixels: compute per-pixel L2 distance to every row in the LUT, take argmin -> index in [0,255]. Divide by 255.0 to get normalized rain-shadow intensity in [0,1].
4. Result: 0 = no rain shadow (windward or flat), 1 = maximum rain shadow (driest leeward zone). Ocean/no-data pixels are the (30,30,30) sentinel, NOT a valid viridis entry (viridis[0] ≈ [68,1,84]).
value_semantics: Min meaningful value ~0 (purple, ~[68,1,84]) = minimal orographic drying; max ~1 (yellow, ~[253,231,37]) = strongest rain shadow. ~77% of pixels are the [30,30,30] ocean/null sentinel. ~18% are the viridis low end (purple land with mild shadow). Yellow hotspots are narrow leeward corridors at mountain crests. No physical units visible; value is a dimensionless shadow index.
integration_notes: To use as a Project-R RAINFALL input: after decoding to [0,1] shadow index, INVERT it (rainfall_proxy = 1 - shadow_index) and write as a single-channel grayscale PNG. Apply the ocean sentinel mask to set ocean pixels to a neutral mid-value (e.g. 0.5) or zero depending on whether coastal runoff should be suppressed. Feed into the rainfall slot; Project-R resamples it to section resolution automatically. This is a secondary option — if a direct absolute-rainfall map exists in the export (e.g. Rainfall.png or Precipitation.png), prefer that; use RainShadow only if no direct rainfall map is available or to modulate a flat rainfall field spatially. Could also serve as a DISPLAY_ONLY overlay on the preview sphere to help the user select rain-shadow terrain sections.
caveats: This is a derived orographic-reduction field, not absolute precipitation — it captures where mountains dry out air masses, not total rainfall. Viridis low end (purple) and the ocean sentinel (dark grey [30,30,30]) are visually very similar at small display sizes; be careful not to confuse them when masking. The 8-bit depth gives only 256 viridis steps, which is adequate for a rainfall weight but not for fine precipitation modelling. Check the export for a sibling Rainfall.png or Precipitation.png — if present, that map is directly usable and makes this one redundant as an erosion driver (keep it only for display or cross-validation).

name: RockType
represents: Geological rock-type / lithology classes across landmasses; ocean is a single near-black fill color (not a data class)
decode_recipe: The analyzer reports 67 unique RGB colors, but visually this is clearly a ~15-20 class categorical map; the extra colors are JPEG/PNG compression fringing at blob edges. Decode steps: (1) Collect all unique RGB triplets, discard any with count < 0.005 * total_pixels as fringe noise. The surviving set is the true palette (~15-20 entries). (2) Map every pixel to its nearest palette entry by minimum Euclidean RGB distance. (3) Assign class IDs 0..N-1 to the palette entries. Class for RGB≈(2,3,33) and its near-black ocean variants (≈(1,3,28), (2,3,38), (2,4,42)) = ocean / no-data mask, class ID 0. (4) Remaining classes are distinct rock types — assign K_sp erodibility values heuristically or from Gleba documentation: bright lime-green, mid-green, dark-green blobs = likely vegetation-covered sedimentary (high K_sp); golden-yellow / tan = limestone or sandstone (high-medium); brown / dark-brown = igneous or laterite (medium-low); blue land patches = possible volcanic/basaltic (low); pink/mauve = metamorphic or salt (low); white = exposed quartzite or ice (very low). No in-image legend is present — class identity must come from Gleba generator source or accompanying metadata.
value_semantics: Each pixel encodes one of ~15-20 discrete rock-type categories via a fixed color palette. Ocean / no-data = RGB≈(2,3,33), comprising 63% of pixels. No physical units; values are categorical labels, not a scalar field. No colorbar or legend is embedded in the image.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), matches the standard Gleba export resolution used by sibling maps
integration_notes: Project-R does not currently consume this map, but it is the best candidate in the export set for a spatial erodibility field K_sp. Integration sketch: on section crop, resample the categorical layer (nearest-neighbor, never bilinear, to preserve class IDs) to the erosion grid resolution. Build a user-editable color->K_sp lookup table (default heuristic values above). Pass the K_sp grid into the stream-power erosion stage where currently K_sp is a single global scalar. The ocean class (≈RGB 2,3,33) also gives a clean land/sea mask as a free byproduct — could be used as the land_sea_mask role to replace the brightness-threshold approach. For section selection, the variety and patchiness of rock types is a useful proxy for geological interest; a future UI control could highlight regions with high lithological diversity.
caveats: No in-image legend — class-to-rock-type mapping requires Gleba generator source or external documentation; without it the K_sp assignments are heuristic guesses. The 67 unique colors include compression fringe artifacts; nearest-color snapping to the true palette is mandatory before any class lookup. The ocean fill is not a uniform single color (four near-black variants visible in top_colors) so the sea mask must use a distance threshold (~15 RGB units from (2,3,33)) rather than an exact match. If a TileType or BiomeType sibling map exists in the same export, it may encode overlapping information (check for redundancy before building two separate erodibility pipelines). Nearest-neighbor resampling is critical — bilinear interpolation will create spurious intermediate colors that break the palette lookup.

name: SinksAndSources
represents: Categorical flow-routing classification: ocean, land, flow sinks (topographic depressions where water cannot drain), flow sources (runoff origin points), and a fifth rare class — pre-computed hydrological network metadata for the planet generator's internal drainage solver
decode_recipe:
Exactly 5 discrete palette entries. Map each pixel by exact RGB match to class:
  [0, 100, 150]   -> class 0: OCEAN        (75.19 % of pixels)
  [80, 80, 80]    -> class 1: LAND         (21.74 %)
  [100, 0, 150]   -> class 2: SINK         (1.86 %)   — drainage depression / coastal pit
  [200, 0, 0]     -> class 3: SOURCE       (1.19 %)   — runoff source / spring point
  [0, 200, 0]     -> class 4: RARE/UNKNOWN (0.02 %)   — extremely sparse, class uncertain

Use nearest-color matching (L2 in RGB space) rather than exact match to be robust to any JPEG re-save artefacts (the file is PNG so exact match is safe here).
value_semantics: No physical scalar units. Pure categorical labels produced by the Gleba planet generator's internal flow-routing pre-pass. Sinks mark depressions that were pit-filled or flagged; sources mark upstream headwater cells. No legend text visible in image. Ocean class aligns with the coastline geometry visible in companion maps.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), matches the standard Gleba export resolution
integration_notes:
Primary extraction: derive a binary LAND/SEA mask by isolating class 0 (OCEAN) pixels. This gives a clean coastline mask usable as the land_sea_mask extension slot in Project-R to define sea level more precisely than a brightness threshold on the heightmap. Implementation: load image, build boolean array (R==0) & (G==100) & (B==150) for ocean pixels, invert for land mask, save as single-channel uint8 PNG alongside the heightmap.

The sink/source annotation (classes 2 and 3) is NOT worth passing to Project-R's erosion pipeline: landlab's FlowAccumulator + DepressionFinderAndRouter already computes its own pit-filling and source detection from the heightmap directly. Importing the planet generator's pre-computed version would be redundant and potentially inconsistent after erosion modifies the surface.

For section-selection guidance the map adds little beyond what the world-color or heightmap already shows. Display-only use on the preview sphere is unattractive (5-color blocky image).
caveats: The land/sea mask derivable here should be cross-checked against TileElevation or the world-color map's ocean regions — Gleba may define "ocean" with a slightly different coastline rasterization than the elevation zero-crossing. The rare green class (0.02%) is ambiguous; treat as LAND for masking purposes. This map carries no elevation, rainfall, or erodibility information and cannot substitute for any of the four primary Project-R inputs.

name: SoilDepth
represents: Soil depth (regolith thickness) over land; black sentinel for ocean/no-data. Thin bright-yellow lines are river/drainage channels where soil thins to zero. Land values ramp from shallow (purple) to deep (yellow) following viridis.
decode_recipe: 1. Mask out ocean sentinel: pixels where RGB == (30,30,30) or within ~2 DN of it are no-data (ocean). 2. For remaining land pixels: build the matplotlib viridis LUT (256 x 3 uint8 entries via `matplotlib.cm.get_cmap('viridis', 256)`). 3. For each land pixel find the nearest LUT entry by Euclidean distance in RGB space → index i in [0,255]. 4. Normalised soil depth = i / 255.0, in [0,1]. 5. No physical unit legend is visible; treat as relative depth only unless Gleba generator metadata supplies a max depth in metres. The analyzer confirms viridis: top non-ocean color is (254,231,36) which matches viridis index 255 to within 1 DN, and secondary cluster around (70,43,121) matches viridis index ~20.
value_semantics: Black (30,30,30) = ocean / no data (~77% of pixels). Purple (viridis low end, index ~0) = shallow soil / bare bedrock. Bright yellow (viridis high end, index ~255) = deepest soil accumulation. Thin yellow filaments = river channels where soil is stripped to zero. No physical unit range is shown; value is a relative scalar in [0,1] after LUT inversion.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), same resolution as the other Gleba exports
integration_notes: Not consumed by Project-R today. Two extension paths: (1) Spatial K_sp erodibility field — thin-soil / bedrock areas (low index) get lower K_sp (harder bedrock), deep-soil areas get higher K_sp (friable regolith); load as a per-pixel multiplier on the base erodibility constant in the stream-power step. (2) Land/sea mask — the (30,30,30) sentinel gives a clean binary land mask without needing a brightness threshold on the heightmap; could replace or cross-check the existing threshold approach. For either use: load with PIL, convert to float32, apply the viridis inverse-LUT to produce a [0,1] scalar array, then resample to section resolution with bilinear interpolation before passing to the erosion kernel.
caveats: 8-bit viridis encoding limits usable precision to ~256 levels; banding may appear in very flat soil-depth regions. No physical units or legend are visible — the [0,1] scalar is relative only unless the Gleba planet-generator config exposes a max_soil_depth parameter. The ocean sentinel (30,30,30) is not true black (0,0,0), so a strict zero-mask would miss it — use a threshold of < 35 in all channels. Soil depth encodes post-weathering regolith state, not rock hardness directly; the K_sp mapping is an approximation and should be validated against the TileElevation heightmap (deep soil tends to accumulate in topographic lows, so K_sp derived from this will partly mirror relief — consider whether that double-counts elevation information).

name: SoilPermeability
represents: Soil permeability (hydraulic conductivity / infiltration rate) over land — how readily water passes through the soil column. Higher values (yellow) = more permeable; lower values (purple/blue) = impermeable or clay-rich soils. Ocean cells are masked with a near-black sentinel.
decode_recipe:
1. Build the matplotlib viridis LUT: `import matplotlib.cm as cm; lut = (cm.get_cmap('viridis', 256)(range(256))[:, :3] * 255).astype(np.uint8)` (shape 256x3).
2. Mask ocean/no-data: pixels where max(R,G,B) <= 32 are ocean sentinel (~(30,30,30)); set those to NaN.
3. For remaining land pixels: for each pixel RGB, find nearest LUT entry by Euclidean distance in RGB space → index i in [0,255].
4. Normalized permeability = i / 255.0, range [0,1], where 0 = minimum permeability (dark purple) and 1 = maximum permeability (bright yellow).
5. No physical units are recoverable from the image (no legend/colorbar visible); treat as a dimensionless [0,1] scalar.
value_semantics: Black/near-black (30,30,30) = ocean/no-data mask (~77% of pixels). Yellow (254,231,36) = highest permeability (~3.7% of pixels, concentrated at coastlines and shallow-soil areas). Purple/blue = lowest permeability (impermeable clay/rock). Green/cyan = intermediate. No physical units visible; scalar is normalized [0,1].
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, confirmed 2:1 aspect ratio, pixel-aligned with other Gleba exports
integration_notes: Project-R has no current slot for permeability. The physically meaningful extension would be as an inverse runoff-concentration modifier feeding into the K_sp erodibility field: high permeability → water infiltrates → less overland flow → lower effective stream power → reduce K_sp locally. This is a second-order correction; it is not a direct erodibility proxy. If implemented, decode to [0,1] scalar, invert (1 - permeability_norm) to get relative runoff fraction, then multiply by a base K_sp to get spatial erodibility. Load alongside the heightmap section crop, resample to erosion grid resolution (typically much coarser). Ocean mask must be applied before any resampling to avoid bleeding sentinel values into coastal land cells.
caveats: The analyzer failed to identify viridis because 77% of pixels are the near-black ocean sentinel (30,30,30), which skews the colormap fit; visual inspection confirms viridis clearly. No legend is present so physical units (e.g. mm/hr, m/day) are unknown — only relative values are recoverable. Permeability is not the same as rock erodibility (K_sp): permeable soils reduce runoff but may erode easily once saturated. Overlaps conceptually with any soil-type or geology map in the same export set; check for a SoilType or RockType sibling before implementing, as those may carry the same information in a more actionable form. 8-bit encoding limits scalar precision to ~256 levels after LUT inversion.

name: SoilRichness
represents: Soil fertility / nutrient richness over land areas of the Gleba planet. Ocean and no-data pixels are flat near-black. Bright yellow-green patches mark the most fertile soil; dark blue-purple marks the least fertile land. Thin white branching lines baked into the ramp layer are the game's river-network overlay.
decode_recipe:
1. Ocean/null mask: any pixel with all three channels <= 35 (the flat RGB ~[30,30,30] background that covers 77% of the image) is ocean — set to NaN or 0.
2. For land pixels: build the matplotlib viridis LUT at 256 steps (import matplotlib.cm; lut = (matplotlib.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0,1,256))[:,:3]*255).astype(np.uint8)). For each land pixel, find the nearest LUT entry by Euclidean RGB distance; its index / 255 gives normalized soil richness in [0, 1]. (The automated cmap fit was inconclusive — cubehelix mean_err 0.121 was best but coverage only 44%. Visual inspection strongly matches viridis: dark-purple low end through cyan to yellow-green high end.)
3. No legend or physical units are visible in the image. The scalar is a dimensionless game-engine fertility value.
value_semantics: Black (RGB ~30,30,30) = ocean / no data (77% of pixels). Dark purple-blue = low soil richness (low index). Cyan-teal = mid richness. Yellow-green = maximum richness (high index). Physical range unknown; scalar is a game-internal [0,1]-ish fertility score. White/near-white thin branching lines on land are river network artifacts baked into the same layer.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, exact 2:1, consistent with the other Gleba exports
integration_notes: No direct slot in Project-R's current pipeline. The most defensible use is section-selection guidance: overlay it on the preview sphere so a user can pick a fertile-looking region to erode. As an erodibility (K_sp) proxy it is a significant semantic stretch — soil richness in a game engine has no calibrated relationship to rock erodibility. If someone did want to wire it in as K_sp, load it, apply the viridis inverse LUT to get [0,1], apply the ocean mask, and feed into the erodibility spatial field slot once that extension is built. More practically, it is a useful world-map layer alongside the color/biome map for display on the sphere.
caveats: 1. River network lines (white/bright streaks) are baked into the ramp layer — they will appear as false high-richness spikes if used as a data field; mask or blur before any numeric use. 2. 8-bit only; 580 unique colors after the viridis ramp is sampled sparsely across the dynamic range, so banding will be visible if upscaled or used as a smooth field. 3. Colormap identification is low-confidence (best automated fit mean_err 0.121); if the game uses a custom LUT the decoded scalar will be nonlinearly distorted. 4. Semantically distant from any erosion parameter — do not confuse with a rainfall or moisture map even though the visual palette and land-coverage pattern are superficially similar.

name: SoilTexture
represents: Discrete soil texture classes (sandy, clayey, silty, mixed etc.) for Gleba's land areas; ocean/no-data is black background
decode_recipe:
1. Define anchor class colors from visual read and top_colors:
   - ID 0 (ocean/no-data): RGB(30, 30, 30)  — 77% of pixels
   - ID 1 (soil class A, bright green): RGB(12, 205, 37)
   - ID 2 (soil class B, red): RGB(253, 0, 0)
   - ID 3 (soil class C, olive/gray-green): RGB(87, 99, 68)
   - ID 4 (soil class D, blue-purple): visually ~RGB(80, 80, 180) — read remaining distinct blobs
2. For each pixel: assign class = argmin Euclidean distance in RGB space to the anchor set.
3. Ocean mask: class 0 (or threshold all channels < 40).
4. To drive K_sp: map class IDs to erodibility scalars, e.g. sandy=high, clay=low, silt=medium.
Note: boundaries between classes are softly blended (hence 29 848 unique colors despite ~5 discrete classes). Nearest-centroid in RGB gives clean class boundaries.
value_semantics: No physical units or legend present in the image. Colors represent game-engine-defined soil texture categories. Black (RGB ~30,30,30) = ocean or no-data. Bright green, red, olive-gray, and blue-purple blobs each map to a distinct soil type. No quantitative range is encoded — this is a class label map, not a scalar ramp.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), standard Gleba export resolution, pixel-aligned with sibling heightmap exports
integration_notes: No current Project-R slot. The only viable extension use is as a spatial erodibility field: map each soil class to a K_sp multiplier (sandy = ~1.5x baseline, clay = ~0.5x, silt = ~1.0x) and resample the class raster to the section grid before the stream-power erosion step. This would require adding a K_sp input slot to the erosion operator. For now it is display-only context at best. It could also guide section selection (pick regions with diverse soil texture for richer erosion outcomes), but that is manual UX, not a data driver. Do not confuse with a rock-type/geology map — this is soil surface texture, which affects surface erodibility, not bedrock incision resistance.
caveats: Analyzer flagged categorical_candidate: false due to 29 848 unique colors, but those are all boundary-blend interpolations between ~5 true classes — the map is genuinely categorical. No legend is embedded; class-to-soil-type mapping must be inferred from Gleba planet generator documentation or by correlating color against known biome/elevation regions. The analyzer's colormap fits (cubehelix etc.) are meaningless here — this is not a ramp. Redundancy: if a geology or rock-type map is present in the export set, that is a stronger erodibility driver than soil texture.

name: TectonicMicroplates
represents: Tectonic microplate segmentation — each irregular blob is one microplate, color is an arbitrary categorical label (plate ID), not a scalar quantity
decode_recipe: The image is a categorical label map with JPEG-style anti-aliasing at plate boundaries, producing ~1711 apparent unique colors from what are ~100-300 true plate colors. To decode: (1) Load as uint8 RGB. (2) Erode each channel by a 5px disk kernel to strip boundary-bleed pixels, setting boundary pixels to a sentinel (e.g. [0,0,0]). (3) Cluster the non-sentinel pixels with k-means (k=200-400, or use DBSCAN on RGB space) to recover the true plate palette. (4) Assign every pixel (including uneroded ones) to its nearest cluster centroid by L2 distance in RGB space. Result: integer plate-ID array [0..N-1]. No colormap LUT inversion is needed — colors carry no ordinal meaning, they are purely nominal IDs. To assign scalar properties (uplift U or erodibility K_sp) to plates: build a plate_id -> value lookup table manually or from auxiliary metadata; then remap the ID array through that LUT.
value_semantics: No physical units encoded in color. Each distinct color = one microplate label. Color hue is arbitrary (orange-brown cluster ~15% of map, blue-purple cluster ~15%, remainder scattered across hue wheel). No legend or colorbar present. Min/max luminance (39-216) reflects color variety, not elevation or any scalar field.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, confirmed 2:1, pixel-aligned with the standard Gleba export grid
integration_notes: Project-R has no current slot for this map. Best extension uses: (1) Spatial uplift field U — plate boundaries (detected as pixels where nearest-plate-ID differs from any neighbor after decoding) are orogenic zones; assign high U to boundary pixels, low U to plate interiors, with optional per-plate age/type variation. (2) Spatial erodibility K_sp — assign different rock hardness per plate class (e.g. oceanic crust plates softer than continental cratons). (3) Section-selection guidance — display on the preview sphere so users can deliberately pick cross-boundary sections to get mountain-range terrain. Implementation: after decode step above, Project-R crops the plate-ID raster to the section rect (same crop/projection pipeline as the heightmap), then maps IDs to a float32 K_sp or U field via a user-editable lookup table in the addon UI.
caveats: Anti-aliasing at plate boundaries means naive unique-color counting gives 1711 colors rather than the true plate count — clustering is required before any categorical use. Plate colors are arbitrary nominal labels; no information is embedded about plate type, age, velocity, or rock type — any physical property assignment must come from external metadata or user input. The map depicts microplates (hundreds of small cells) rather than the ~15 major Earth-scale plates, so boundary density is very high and boundary-uplift zones will cover a large fraction of any section. No land/sea distinction is encoded here — ocean and continental plates are mixed indistinguishably. Check sibling exports for a dedicated geology or crust-age map that may carry richer physical information for the same purpose.

name: TectonicPlates
represents: Tectonic plate segmentation — each distinct color identifies one rigid lithospheric plate. 16 plates total, covering the full globe with no gaps (ocean and continental crust both labeled).
decode_recipe: Build a 16-entry palette table from the top_colors list (exact RGB values: e.g. [202,113,2], [227,159,67], [30,214,90], [2,190,131], [223,82,172], [53,173,58], [31,57,215], [100,9,244], [8,165,139], [135,41,153], [26,42,110], [221,216,174], plus the remaining 4 minor colors). For each pixel, find the nearest-color entry in the palette (Euclidean RGB distance) and assign its 0-based plate_id (0–15). Output is a uint8 label image. Colors carry no scalar meaning — they are arbitrary plate identifiers only. No colormap LUT needed.
value_semantics: Each pixel value after decoding is an integer plate ID in [0, 15]. No physical units. The largest plate (ID mapped to RGB [202,113,2], burnt orange) covers ~29% of the globe. There is no intrinsic ordering — IDs are nominal, not ordinal.
aligned_equirect: yes, 4096x2048 (2:1 aspect confirmed)
integration_notes: Project-R does not consume this map directly. Two extension paths: (1) UPLIFT driver U — compute a plate-boundary mask (dilate each plate label map, XOR adjacent-plate pixels), then apply a distance transform to produce a continuous "proximity to plate boundary" scalar in [0,1]; feed that into the K_sp/U slot. Convergent vs divergent boundary type cannot be inferred from this map alone without a separate velocity or boundary-type export. A simple all-boundary proxy still gives geologically plausible orogeny at the correct locations. (2) SECTION SELECTION guidance — plate boundaries define geologically interesting regions to crop; a UI overlay highlighting boundary zones could help the user pick sections with active mountain-building. Do NOT use as a world_map display layer — the arbitrary rainbow palette would be confusing to the end user. To implement uplift: load label image, build adjacency mask (scipy.ndimage label or skimage), distance-transform from boundary pixels, normalize, write as float32 greyscale PNG aligned to the heightmap.
caveats: Colors are arbitrary and may vary between Gleba export runs — do not hardcode the palette; always re-derive it from the actual file. No boundary-type information (subduction vs rift vs transform) is encoded, so uplift magnitude cannot be differentiated by boundary type without additional exports. The 16-plate count covers both oceanic and continental crust with no distinction, which limits geological specificity. Check whether a companion CrustType or OceanicCrust map exists in the export to disambiguate continental vs oceanic plates — that combination would improve erodibility and sea-level masking significantly.

name: TileElevationColorSmooth
represents: Elevation rendered as a custom hypsometric tint (multi-stop color ramp): deep ocean = dark navy, ocean = mid-blue, shallow/shelf = cyan-blue, lowland = green, mid-elevation = yellow-green/cream, high elevation = tan/orange, peaks = dark brown/near-black, polar snow/ice caps = white-gray. Smoothed interpolation applied (vs the raw tile-grid version).
decode_recipe: This is a custom hypsometric tint palette specific to the Gleba generator — not a standard matplotlib colormap (analyzer returned likely_colormap=null; best cmap fit RdBu mean_err=0.097 is too poor to trust for inversion). Do NOT recover elevation from this image. For display-only use: load as sRGB, no transform. If approximate elevation recovery is unavoidable, build a manual LUT from the visual breakpoints: (9,56,96) = ocean floor/min, mid-blues (~30,80,140) = ocean, (~30,160,180) = shallow, (~60,160,80) = lowland, (~180,200,120) = mid, (~220,180,100) = high, (~160,80,30) = very high, (~30,10,10) = peak, (220,230,240) = polar — map each pixel to nearest LUT entry to get a rank; rescale to physical elevation range if known. Error will be substantial. Use TileElevation grayscale sibling for real elevation data.
value_semantics: Black/dark-navy = lowest (deep ocean), white/light-gray = highest (polar caps or peaks). No numeric units encoded; the colormap is aesthetic, not calibrated to metres. The full dynamic range spans deep-ocean trench depth to mountain peaks. No legend visible in the image.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), pixel-aligned with the other TileElevation* siblings
integration_notes: Load directly into the WORLD MAP slot (sRGB, no decoding). It is visually attractive and will render well on the preview sphere — the hypsometric tint gives the user immediate land/sea/mountain context when picking a section. No further transform needed. Do not wire into the HEIGHTMAP slot; use the companion grayscale TileElevation export instead (16-bit preferred). If no grayscale sibling is available, a rough land_sea_mask could be extracted by thresholding the blue channel (B gt 130 and G lt 100 as a rough ocean test), but that is fragile near coastal shelves and should be a fallback only.

name: TileElevationColorSmoothIceAge
represents: Full-planet hypsometric tint combining land elevation, ocean bathymetry, and ice-age polar ice extents, rendered with a custom Earth-style multi-segment color ramp
decode_recipe: Load as sRGB RGB — no scalar extraction. This is a display-only map. The color encodes elevation via a custom multi-segment hypsometric LUT that is not invertible to a usable scalar field: the best matplotlib fit (RdBu, mean_err=0.094) is far too poor for reliable inversion. Color segments observed: dark navy [9,56,95] = deep ocean; medium blue [11-12,63-65,107-110] = mid-ocean; light cyan [215,255,255] (dominant, 19.5%) = shallow shelf and polar sea ice; white [255,255,255] = glaciated peaks and polar ice sheets; green tones = vegetated lowlands; tan/beige = mid-elevation plains; brown/red-brown = high terrain. If elevation scalars are needed, use the companion grayscale TileElevation* map instead.
value_semantics: Qualitative color only — no numeric units recoverable without the generator's exact LUT. Visual range: deep ocean (darkest blue) through bathymetric gradient to shoreline, then land from sea-level green through tan plains to brown highlands to white mountain peaks. The ice-age variant adds expanded polar ice sheets (white/gray/light-blue) across both polar strips (~top 8% and bottom 12% of the image). No legend or colorbar visible in the image.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, confirmed 2:1 aspect, pixel-aligned with the heightmap family
integration_notes: Slot directly as the WORLD MAP texture on the Blender preview sphere (sRGB, load as-is, no decode step). This is the most visually informative of the elevation color variants: land/ocean contrast and terrain relief are immediately readable, giving the user strong geographic context when drawing a section. The IceAge ice extents clearly mark the polar regions, which helps users avoid selecting heavily ice-distorted polar sections. Do NOT feed into the heightmap, rainfall, or bathymetry slots — a companion grayscale TileElevation map must supply actual elevation data. Potential extension: a land/sea threshold applied to this image's blue-vs-non-blue pixels could approximate a land/sea mask, but a dedicated binary mask map is far cleaner if available.
caveats: (1) 8-bit RGB only — zero elevation precision; the companion grayscale TileElevation* map is required for all data-driven erosion inputs. (2) IceAge variant — polar ice sheets are larger than in the non-IceAge sibling (TileElevationColorSmooth); pick whichever matches the intended world epoch and use the same epoch consistently across all map slots. (3) Custom hypsometric LUT is not a standard matplotlib colormap, making scalar inversion impractical — do not attempt to reconstruct elevation from pixel color. (4) The dominant color [215,255,255] at 19.5% of pixels spans both polar ice and shallow-water shelves — confirms the ramp is multi-segment and non-monotone, reinforcing that scalar recovery is unreliable. (5) Redundant with TileElevationColorSmooth (non-ice-age sibling) — only one is needed as the world map; the other is informational.

name: TileElevationColorSmoothNoIce
represents: Hypsometric-tint elevation visualization of the Gleba planet surface — elevation encoded as a continuous color ramp applied to smoothed terrain, with no polar-ice overlay. Dark navy = deep ocean, blue = shallows, cyan = coastal/very-shallow, green = lowland, yellow-white = plateau/upland, red-brown = high mountains, near-black = extreme peaks.
decode_recipe: This is a display-only RGB render of elevation using a custom hypsometric LUT — NOT a standard matplotlib colormap (best cmap fit is gist_earth at mean_err 0.137, which is too loose to invert reliably). Do NOT attempt luminance-based extraction. To recover scalar elevation, use the sibling single-channel TileElevation grayscale map instead. If this map must be decoded: (1) obtain the exact Gleba planet-generator hypsometric LUT (256-entry RGB table); (2) for each pixel, find nearest LUT entry by Euclidean distance in RGB space; (3) use that index/255 as the normalized elevation in [0,1]; (4) rescale to physical units if the planet's elevation range is known. Without the exact LUT this will produce artefacts — use the grayscale sibling.
value_semantics: No legend embedded in the image. Color ramp runs: deep navy (RGB ~9,57,96, ~47% of pixels = deep ocean floor) through blue (shallow ocean), cyan (coastal shallows), green (lowland), yellow-white (plateaus), red (high terrain), dark brown/near-black (peak elevations). Absolute elevation range unknown from this file alone — infer from sibling grayscale heightmap. The "Smooth" tag implies low-frequency elevation smoothing was applied before colorizing; fine relief detail is reduced relative to raw TileElevation.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), standard equirectangular, pixel-aligned with sibling TileElevation maps
integration_notes: Load directly as the WORLD MAP slot (sRGB, decoded as-is). It gives the preview sphere a visually informative Earth-like appearance that lets the user immediately identify continents, ocean basins, and mountain chains when picking a section. No color-space transform needed — treat as display RGB. Do NOT use as heightmap input; the custom hypsometric ramp cannot be cleanly inverted. Wire the grayscale TileElevation sibling into the HEIGHTMAP slot instead. At 4096x2048 it will load efficiently and downsample well for the sphere preview.
caveats: 1. Redundancy: this is purely a visual derivative of the TileElevation data — it adds no independent information beyond what the grayscale heightmap already captures. 2. "Smooth" variant: elevation has been low-pass filtered, so fine topographic detail is suppressed compared to an unsmoothed TileElevation — do not attempt to invert it for erosion seeding. 3. "NoIce" variant: a companion with-ice variant may exist; for worlds with polar ice caps the iced version may look more realistic on the preview sphere, but for erosion purposes the NoIce surface is the correct land-surface input. 4. Only 1779 unique colors despite 8 MP — heavy color quantization from 8-bit LUT; elevation recovered from this would have coarse banding (~256 levels max). 5. The custom hypsometric ramp is not a named standard colormap so automated LUT-inversion pipelines cannot be applied without the generator's palette table.

name: TileElevationGreyscale
represents: Planet surface elevation — continuous scalar field, darker = lower (ocean floor / sea), lighter = higher (land / mountains)
decode_recipe: Open with PIL in mode I;16 (or equivalent 16-bit loader). Cast to float32/float64. Divide by 65535.0 to get normalized elevation in [0, 1]. Multiply by max_elevation_m to recover metres (no legend visible; assume ~8000–10000 m for earthlike scale, or calibrate against a sibling TileElevation map that carries a physical range). Black (value ~0) = deepest ocean / minimum; near-white (max observed 53015/65535 ≈ 0.809) = highest peaks. No colormap inversion needed — luminance is monotonically proportional to elevation.
value_semantics: uint16 0 = minimum elevation (ocean floor / datum); uint16 53015 (observed max, ~81% of range) = highest terrain; mean ~23095 (~35% of range). frac_zero 0.09% — almost no true-zero pixels, so ocean floor sits slightly above 0. 35765 unique levels: genuine continuous 16-bit precision throughout. No physical unit legend visible in the image.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), standard Gleba export resolution. Pixel-aligned with sibling exports in the same folder.
integration_notes: Load directly into Project-R's heightmap slot. Decode: `elev = (np.array(Image.open(path), dtype=np.float32)) / 65535.0 * max_elev_m`. Sea level threshold: inspect the bimodal histogram (major ocean peak bins 3–4 → uint16 ~12000–20000; land peak bins 7–8 → ~28000–36000); a threshold around uint16 24000–26000 cleanly separates ocean from land and can derive a land/sea mask if no dedicated mask map is present. The sharp black coastline outlines visible in the image (1–2 px wide, value near 0) are artefacts of the planet generator; consider a small morphological dilation or median filter at the coastline before feeding to stream-power erosion, or they will seed spurious deep incision channels exactly at the shore.
caveats: 1) Physical elevation range unknown (no legend): max_elev_m must be set by the user or inferred from a companion map. 2) Thin black coastline-outline artefacts (~1-2 px) at every land/sea boundary — these are not real troughs and will create erosion artefacts if unmasked. 3) The Gleba export folder likely contains multiple TileElevation* variants (colour-shaded, colourmap, etc.); this greyscale 16-bit version is the authoritative data source — the coloured siblings are display-only and should not be used as a heightmap instead. 4) The 8-bit top_colors readout (99.89% white) is a PIL I→RGB scaling artefact and does not reflect actual pixel distribution — trust n_unique_levels and lum_hist16 instead.

name: TileElevationGreyscaleBathymetry
represents: Combined land elevation + ocean-floor bathymetry encoded as a single 16-bit grayscale scalar field; brighter = higher land, mid-gray = shallower/deeper ocean floor, black = deepest ocean
decode_recipe: 1. Open with PIL in mode I;16 or numpy as uint16 — do NOT convert to 8-bit first. 2. Raw pixel v in [0, 65535]. No colormap; value is the scalar directly. 3. Determine sea-level threshold: the histogram has a gap around bin 6 (~24576-28672) with only 112 k pixels, then a large ocean-floor peak in bins 7-9 (~29k-41k). Sea level sits near v = 28672 (44% of 65535) — cross-check against TileElevationGreyscale (land-only sibling) or a land-mask map to pin it precisely. 4. Land pixels (v > sea_level_v): elevation_m = (v - sea_level_v) / (65535 - sea_level_v) * max_land_elev_m. 5. Ocean pixels (v <= sea_level_v): depth_m = (sea_level_v - v) / sea_level_v * max_ocean_depth_m. 6. For Project-R heightmap slot, use v/65535 directly (brightness = relative elevation across full range) and set sea-level fraction accordingly in the addon.
value_semantics: v=65535 (white) = highest land peak; v=0 (black) = deepest ocean trench; sea level approximately at v~28672-32768 (needs calibration). Mean v=45488 (~69% of max) reflects land-heavy / high-plateau planet. frac_zero=0.09% means almost no pixels are at absolute minimum — deep ocean is sparse. 40135 unique 16-bit levels confirms full-precision continuous data, not quantized.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, exact 2:1
integration_notes: HEIGHTMAP slot: load as uint16 numpy array, pass v/65535 as the elevation field. This is the preferred heightmap input — 16-bit gives 40k+ unique levels, avoiding the banding that would afflict an 8-bit grayscale. BATHYMETRY slot: extract ocean pixels (v less than sea_level_v), remap (sea_level_v - v) / sea_level_v to [0,1] so white = deepest, then supply to the continental-shelf/sea-floor pass. One file thus fills both slots. Recommended extension: derive a land/sea binary mask at the same sea-level threshold to feed a future LAND_SEA_MASK slot, avoiding a brightness-threshold approximation.
caveats: 1. The visual shows thin black coastline/plate-boundary outlines drawn into the pixel data; these will appear as artificial sharp trenches in eroded output — compare against TileElevationGreyscale to check if that sibling lacks them. 2. Sea-level threshold is not labeled anywhere in the file; must be inferred from the histogram valley or diffed against a land-only sibling. 3. The 8-bit projection collapses to only 31 distinct levels and shows 99.89% white — always load as 16-bit uint16 or information is destroyed. 4. Bimodal histogram (ocean-floor cluster in bins 7-9, land cluster in bin 15) is characteristic of combined elevation+bathymetry encoding; do not treat as a pure land heightmap without handling the sub-sea-level range separately. 5. Redundant with TileElevationGreyscale — that sibling likely has ocean at a flat value; use this one when bathymetry depth matters, the other when a clean zero-ocean surface is preferred for erosion seeding.

name: TileElevationGreyscaleLand
represents: Land surface elevation only; ocean pixels are hard-zeroed (masked out). Encodes terrain height above sea level for continental landmasses. The near-white fringe at coastlines is the transition from zero ocean to elevated terrain.
decode_recipe: 1. Open with PIL in mode 'I' (16-bit). 2. Convert to numpy uint16 array, shape (2048, 4096). 3. Normalize: elev_norm = pixel_value / 65535.0 — gives [0, 1] relative elevation. 4. Ocean mask: land_mask = (pixel_value > 0). Zero pixels are ocean and must be treated as sea level (not zero elevation on land). 5. To recover physical elevation in metres, multiply elev_norm by the planet's max elevation (unknown from file alone; use the companion TileElevation metadata or treat max raw value 40496/65535 ≈ 0.617 as the ceiling and scale accordingly). No colormap inversion needed — it is a direct linear grayscale.
value_semantics: min=0 (ocean, masked); max=40496 raw uint16 (highest peak, ~61.7% of the 16-bit ceiling). mean=702 raw (low because 77.2% of pixels are ocean zeros). Brighter = higher elevation. No embedded legend; physical units (metres) are unknown without the planet generator's elevation scale parameter.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (exactly 2:1); matches the standard Gleba export resolution
integration_notes: Primary heightmap slot: load as uint16, normalize to [0,1] by dividing by 65535 (or by 40496 to stretch land range to full [0,1]). Feed directly into the section crop + Hammer projection pipeline. The zero-ocean mask is a free bonus: derive land_sea_mask via `pixel_value > 0` — use this to seed the coastal erosion stage's shoreline boundary rather than computing a brightness threshold. Because ocean cells are zero and indistinguishable from flat sea-level land, do NOT run stream-power erosion across the whole raster without first applying the land mask; otherwise flat zero-ocean regions will generate spurious drainage. Clip eroded output back to the land mask before reassembly. This map does not carry bathymetry — pair with a companion TileElevation (full, non-Land) or a dedicated bathymetry export for the sea-floor/continental-shelf pass.
caveats: 1. Ocean-zeroed: cannot drive the bathymetry slot; the full TileElevationGreyscale (without the Land suffix) is the better choice if it exists in the export, as it should contain sub-sea-level depth values. 2. Physical scale unknown: max raw value 40496 does not map to a known metre ceiling without the generator's metadata; erosion calibration (K_sp, U units) will need a manual scale guess or the metadata file. 3. 77.2% zero pixels mean histogram statistics are dominated by ocean; do not use the image mean/std for normalization without first masking ocean. 4. 16-bit PNG is ideal for erosion (no 8-bit banding), but verify the loader actually reads in 16-bit mode — PIL's default Image.open() may silently downcast to 8-bit; use Image.open().convert('I') or rawarray mode explicitly.

name: TileSlope
represents: Terrain surface slope magnitude (steepness), derived from the elevation field. Ocean/flat pixels are flagged with a sentinel gray; land pixels ramp through the viridis colormap from low slope (purple) to high slope (cyan/teal at the visible maximum).
decode_recipe: 1. Build the matplotlib viridis LUT: `lut = (plt.get_cmap('viridis')(np.linspace(0,1,256))[:,:3]*255).astype(np.uint8)` — shape (256,3). 2. Create an ocean/no-data mask: pixels where all(|ch - 30| <= 3) are masked out (77% of image; they are a sentinel that does not sit on the viridis ramp). 3. For each unmasked pixel, find nearest LUT entry by L2 distance in RGB space -> index i in [0,255]. slope_normalized = i / 255.0, range [0,1] (0 = flat land, 1 = steepest slope visible in the dataset). 4. Physical units are not recoverable from the image (no legend/colorbar present); treat as a dimensionless slope proxy. Note: only the lower ~40-50% of the viridis ramp appears to be used (purple through cyan); no yellow/green end is visible, so maximum slopes are moderate.
value_semantics: Sentinel [30,30,30] = ocean or zero-slope (no data). Land pixels: viridis index 0 (purple, ~[68,1,84]) = lowest slope; viridis index ~120-130 (cyan/teal) = highest slope in this export. No physical units (degrees or radians) are recoverable — no legend is present in the image. Mean luminance of 31.9 (barely above the 30.0 sentinel) reflects that 77% of the map is ocean.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, 2:1 aspect, matches the standard Gleba export resolution
integration_notes: Project-R computes slope internally from the heightmap (TileElevation*) during erosion, so this map is redundant as an erosion driver. The only practical uses are: (a) display_only on the preview sphere as a shaded-relief-like overlay; (b) section_selection — high-slope regions (cyan fringe pixels at mountain ridges and steep coastlines) are the most geomorphologically interesting targets for erosion runs, so a user-visible slope overlay could guide where to draw the section box. Do NOT use as a heightmap substitute — it encodes slope not elevation. If an erodibility extension (K_sp) is implemented later, slope-proxy could be a very weak heuristic input, but a lithology/rock-type map would be far more appropriate. Load with Pillow in RGB mode, apply the viridis inverse LUT, mask the sentinel before any spatial analysis.
caveats: Fully derived from TileElevation (or whichever elevation layer was used to generate it) — carries no independent information beyond what the heightmap already contains. Physical units (degrees/radians/rise-over-run) are unrecoverable without the generator's legend. The sentinel value [30,30,30] is ambiguous (could also be a very-low-slope-but-valid land cell at index ~0 on the ramp, though visually it blankets the entire ocean). Only the bottom half of the viridis ramp is populated, compressing dynamic range. No ice-age vs no-ice variant concern applies to a slope map.

name: TrueColor
represents: Stylized sRGB true-color planet surface visualization: dark navy ocean, green vegetation, sandy/tan desert, reddish-brown bare mountains, white polar ice caps — analogous to a NASA "Blue Marble"-style composite but rendered by the Gleba planet generator.
decode_recipe: Load as sRGB, use pixel values directly. No LUT inversion, no colormap lookup. Ocean is a very dark saturated navy (~[10-15, 14-25, 54-70] RGB); land varies from green (~[30-80, 80-140, 30-80]) to sandy tan (~[180-230, 180-220, 100-160]) to bare brown/red for high terrain; polar caps are near-white ([210-230, 210-230, 210-230]). For a derived binary land/sea mask: classify pixels as ocean where B > 40 AND B > 2*R AND B > 1.8*G (tuned to this dark-navy palette), else land.
value_semantics: No physical scalar encoded. Colors are display aesthetic: navy = open ocean; green = vegetated land; tan/beige = arid/desert; brownish-red = bare high terrain; near-white = polar ice/snow; light gray fringe at extreme poles. No colorbar or legend present.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, exact 2:1 aspect, matches the standard Gleba export resolution used by all sibling maps in this export set.
integration_notes: Primary role: plug directly into the World Map slot (sRGB, decode-on-load = none). It will render on the preview sphere immediately and gives the user excellent visual context for section selection — continent shapes, desert vs forest zones, and polar extents are all clearly legible. Secondary/extension role: derive a land/sea mask on-the-fly from the RGB values (see decode recipe) and feed it into a future LAND_SEA_MASK slot to define sea level precisely instead of using a brightness threshold on the heightmap. The ocean is planet-spanning (~60% of pixels by top-color analysis) so the mask signal is strong. No resampling needed for the world-map role. For the mask derivation, a single-pass numpy op over the loaded array is sufficient; no PIL palette required.
caveats: 8-bit only — banding is irrelevant for a display image but means this cannot substitute for the heightmap. Contains zero elevation information. The ocean color is an unusually dark navy (min luminance ~15), not standard cerulean, so any generic "blue-channel threshold" land/sea code written for other planet generators will need retuning. The stylized rendering means coastline pixels can have mixed colors (anti-aliased edge blending), so a hard mask will have a 1-2 pixel ragged fringe — erode/dilate before use as a mask. Redundancy: if a dedicated LandSea or OceanMask export exists in the same export set, prefer that over deriving from TrueColor.

name: Vegetation
represents: Vegetation density / plant cover index over land surfaces; ocean is masked to near-black (~30,30,30).
decode_recipe: 1. Ocean mask: pixels where all three channels < 25 are ocean (set scalar = NaN or 0). These account for ~77% of the image (the near-black RGB 30,30,30 background). 2. For remaining land pixels, convert RGB to HSV. The hue encodes the scalar position along a blue→green→yellow→red ramp (no standard matplotlib colormap matched; best fit was cubehelix at mean_err=0.11, too poor to trust). Use hue as a proxy scalar: scalar = clamp((240 - H_degrees) / 240, 0, 1), where H=240° (blue) maps to 0 (sparse/no vegetation) and H=0°/360° (red) maps to 1 (dense vegetation). Dark-interior land patches (HSV value < 0.15) where hue is ambiguous should be treated as either very low or very high — inspect against a known biome region to confirm which end of the ramp they occupy. 3. Alternatively, if a reference color bar from the exporter is available, build a 256-entry LUT from its sampled stops and do nearest-color lookup.
value_semantics: Black/near-black (RGB ~0–25) = ocean, no data. Blue = low vegetation (sparse, coastal, tundra-like). Green = moderate. Yellow/orange = high. Red = peak density. Dark patches inside continental interiors are either deserts (lowest end of ramp, scalar ≈ 0) or highest oversaturation — visual inspection suggests they are low-vegetation dry cores (deserts) within otherwise high-vegetation belts. No physical units or legend visible; scalar is dimensionless [0, 1].
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, exact 2:1 aspect ratio, pixel-aligned with the other Gleba exports in this folder.
integration_notes: No current Project-R slot accepts vegetation data. Two extension paths exist: (a) Spatial erodibility K_sp — invert the scalar (high vegetation = lower K_sp, roots armour soil); load at erosion time, resample to section resolution, multiply against the base K_sp constant. (b) Section-selection guidance only — display on the preview sphere so the user can identify lush vs arid regions to target. Do not use as a RAINFALL proxy; this export set almost certainly includes a dedicated precipitation/humidity map which is a more direct erosion driver. The colormap is non-standard, so the hue-based decode above is an approximation; validate by checking a pixel known to be dense tropical forest (should decode near 1.0).
caveats: No standard matplotlib colormap fits (best mean_err 0.11 over a 47% ramp coverage), so pixel→scalar inversion is approximate. The ambiguity of dark interior patches (desert vs maximum-vegetation saturation) must be resolved before using the scalar quantitatively. If the export pack includes a separate precipitation or humidity map, that map will be strictly more useful for all erosion-driver roles. Vegetation is a lagging ecological indicator and does not directly encode rock erodibility — the K_sp extension use is indirect at best. 8-bit depth means only 256 quantization levels, acceptable for a soft spatial field but not for any primary terrain data.

name: Volcanism
represents: Per-pixel volcanism intensity / tectonic activity level, with discrete intensity classes and sparse point markers for active volcanic hotspots along plate boundaries
decode_recipe: Nearest-color palette lookup to class id. Confirmed palette (all 10 colors): (30,30,30)->0 background/ocean/no-volcanism (77%); (80,80,80)->1 moderate volcanism / continental land (23%); (250,0,0)->2 high volcanism hotspot / active volcanic zone (0.06%); (0,250,50)->3 secondary volcanic marker (0.01%); (255,255,255)->4 peak/special marker (trace); (62,0,0)->5 attenuated red hotspot; (0,62,12)->6 attenuated green marker; (62,63,63)->7 transitional gray; (62,37,0)->8 brownish transition; (250,150,0)->9 orange volcanic marker (all trace). Assign scalar weight 0/1/2 (or 0.0/0.5/1.0) for classes 0/1/2 to produce a continuous uplift-proxy ramp if needed. Use nearest-color (L2 in RGB) rather than channel thresholds due to the near-neutral grays.
value_semantics: No physical units shown; purely relative ordinal. Dark (30,30,30) = quiescent/ocean = 0 volcanism. Medium gray (80,80,80) = continental / low-moderate volcanism. Red (250,0,0) = active volcanic hotspot / high volcanism. Green (0,250,50) = distinct secondary volcanic marker (possibly different eruption style or hydrothermal). White (255,255,255) = peak intensity or special boundary marker. Red/green dots visually trace a ring-of-fire pattern along southern and western continental margins.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048 (2:1), matches the standard Gleba export resolution
integration_notes: Not a direct erosion input. Two extension uses: (1) Spatial UPLIFT field U — reclassify palette classes 0/1/2 to a 0–1 scalar (ocean=0, land=0.3, hotspot=1.0) and feed into the stream-power uplift term U so volcanic zones build relief faster than stable cratons. Load with nearest-color decode, then bicubic resample to section resolution. (2) Section-selection guidance — overlay class-2 (red) pixels on the preview sphere so the user can deliberately pick volcanic arc sections for geologically interesting erosion runs. No blending with heightmap or rainfall; treat as a separate property layer. If future versions expose a K_sp erodibility field, note that volcanic rock is moderately soft (basalt weathers faster than granite) — class 1 land could carry a slightly elevated K_sp.
caveats: Only 10 discrete levels — this is ordinal/categorical, not a continuous scalar; the analyzer's grayscale_continuous verdict is wrong. The two dominant classes (dark/gray) occupy 99.9% of pixels; the colored hotspot markers are sparse point features at sub-0.1% coverage, so any resampling must use nearest-neighbor to preserve them (bilinear would smear red into gray). No legend or physical unit range is embedded. Redundancy check: if sibling exports include a TectonicActivity or PlateStress map, that may carry the same information at higher fidelity — verify before using both as uplift drivers.

name: Waterbodies
represents: Binary land/ocean classification with individually color-labeled inland waterbodies (lakes, ponds, rivers). Two dominant classes cover 99.6% of pixels; scattered colored pixels each encode a unique waterbody ID.
decode_recipe: Check if pixel is grayscale: abs(R-G) < 4 AND abs(R-B) < 4. If grayscale: mean < 55 → class 0 (ocean); mean ≥ 55 → class 1 (land). If not grayscale: assign a unique integer waterbody ID by mapping the exact RGB tuple to a sequential index (one color per connected waterbody feature). No colormap LUT inversion needed — colors are arbitrary per-feature labels, not a ramp.
value_semantics: Black/near-black (30,30,30): ocean — 76.7% of pixels. Mid-gray (80,80,80): land — 22.9% of pixels. Colored non-grayscale pixels (~0.36%): individual inland waterbodies, each unique RGB = one waterbody instance (no physical unit, no consistent colormap — purely an ID label). No legend visible; no physical range inferable from color.
aligned_equirect: yes — 4096x2048, standard 2:1 equirect, pixel-aligned with the other Gleba exports
integration_notes: To extract a binary land/sea mask: threshold mean(R,G,B) at 55 — pixels below are ocean (0), above are land (1). This mask could feed Project-R's planned land_sea_mask extension slot to define sea level precisely rather than relying on a brightness threshold on the heightmap. The waterbody ID layer (colored pixels) is not actionable without a companion legend mapping color → waterbody type/name; ignore it unless that metadata becomes available. Load as a single-channel uint8 after the grayscale extraction step; no resampling needed at 4096x2048.
caveats: Redundant with the heightmap: any pixel below sea-level elevation already implies ocean, making this mask largely superfluous unless the heightmap has ambiguous sea-level calibration. The analyzer verdict of grayscale_continuous is misleading — the image is effectively two-class categorical (the two gray values are discrete, not a ramp). The colored waterbody IDs carry no usable metadata without a separate legend file; their spatial extent is tiny (0.36% of pixels). No rainfall, erodibility, or elevation information present.
